a_rows_sample.anchor: Vocabulary collision — flagged, unresolved. `024119` leads the projection count (49) but uses "projection" in the **CQRS read-model** sense, not the epistemic sense.
a_rows_sample.statement: The C-15-relevant material splits across two corpus regions: Retraction/withdrawal is concentrated in the early/ORIGINAL region (114358, 233040, 111647, 113410, 123619), while Projection is concentrated in the late/extraction era (110525, 140251, 135642, 155035); Temporal spans both. Consequence: the retraction evidence is the project's own thinking while the projection evidence is almost entirely extraction-era — they do not carry equal weight, and a synthesis merging them flattens this distinction. A vocabulary collision is flagged: document 024119 leads the projection keyword count (49) but uses 'projection' in the CQRS read-model sense, not the epistemic sense — a 'Vāṇī-class hazard' requiring separation before any projection synthesis. Three HPA-asked questions the corpus does not visibly answer: can two projections differ without knowledge differing? does absence from a projection mean anything? is history part of the object or a record of transitions?

a_rows_sample.anchor: Session 1 should be the **research/extraction track**. Session 2 should remain the **formal adjudication track**. ... the two streams should **not contaminate each other**.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes a two-track separation: Session 1 (brainstorming corpus -> document-by-document extraction -> Knowledge -> Knowledge Space -> KnowledgeOS -> Kernel concepts -> research synthesis) versus Session 2 (current Kernel law -> F-CM/C-items -> falsification -> adjudication -> rulings), which must not contaminate each other; explicitly freezes Session 2 (including C-15 refinement) until the research extraction catches up. Six-layer target: (1) what did we originally think (Phase 1), (2) what did research introduce (Phase 2), (3) what contradictions appeared, (4) what concepts survived both phases, (5) what remains genuinely unresolved, (6) only then — what, if anything, belongs in the KnowledgeOS Kernel (the output of the exercise, not its starting assumption).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Now we can ask whether **retraction is actually a lifecycle concern**, or whether it is better understood as a consequence of temporal epistemic evolution. But **we should not decide that yet**.
a_rows_sample.statement: Connects the Knowledge extraction's Knowledge-Space/participant/information-at-t/projection/knowledge-at-t/later-information/revision-contraction-supersession pipeline to C-15: raises whether retraction is actually a lifecycle concern or better understood as a consequence of temporal epistemic evolution, explicitly deferring the decision — exactly why extracting Knowledge first, before continuing C-15 refinement, was the right call.

a_rows_sample.statement: Terminological-only collisions separated from genuine contradictions: 'projection' now has three unmergeable senses — A CQRS/read-model projection (024119, 49 hits, leads the cluster count), B epistemic projection of a Knowledge Space (110525, 140251, 135642), C a measure over (Ω,F) (181038, contested by 181719, since sense C is a formalization of B that may not be valid). Also: 'C-1' collision resolved via W:/⟨⟩ prefixes; 'AMBIGUOUS' collision (intent-resolution mechanism outcome vs proposed epistemic state) kept separate, only the latter is constitutional; 'agent' collision (epistemic participant including wires/buffers vs accountable actor) remains unresolved — 'a wire cannot be accountable.'

b_rows_sample.statement: A full relationship table across all thirteen concepts, using four typed relations (contains = container relation, references = a pointer, generates = produces a new instance, depends on = cannot be understood without). b_rows_sample.statement: Three reviewer challenges: (1) 'Archetype' replaces 'nine kinds' until MM-1, since 'archetype' already exists in the corpus (RQ-002) so the rename mints nothing — a ubiquitous-language decision, decided with governance (MM-1), not unilaterally; (2) CONTAINER is demoted from CONFIRMED to CANDIDATE by the author's own admission rule: 'Containers generate Projections' is observed in exactly one space (the EKP's knowledge-graph.php), n=1, and nesting is unevidenced (H-3) — the settling test is a second generating space (confirms) or a capability-plus-scope reduction (refutes); (3) PURPOSE, possibly more fundamental than Container, is flagged not resolved, since the mission is enacted and unratified (D-5 pending), and deepening PURPOSE before ratification would model ahead of the domain expert — recorded as hypothesis U-ONT-2, n=0.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What exists instead ... FOUR DISTINCT PARTIAL ORDERS, one per relationship type: AUTHORITY · PRODUCTION · REALIZATION · CONTAINMENT
b_rows_sample.statement: Four evidenced partial orders replace the refuted single stack: AUTHORITY (who justifies whom) PURPOSE->STRATEGY->PRINCIPLE->DP-n->CAPABILITY; PRODUCTION (who produces whom) PROCESS->Knowledge/Artifacts/Evidence, CAPABILITY->Evidence, CONTAINER->Projection (n=1); REALIZATION (concept -> executable/persistent form) KNOWLEDGE->ARTIFACT (I-1), CAPABILITY->RUNTIME ASSET (R-7, SC-6 gap); CONTAINMENT (what moves together) CONTAINER contains Artifacts (contains other spaces? H-3 open). The intuition underneath the stack survives: relations are directional, with DOMAIN/KNOWLEDGE conceptual and RUNTIME/ARTIFACT realized; but 'which is above' is only answerable per relation, not for the stack as a whole.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge is always knowledge-at-a-time within an evolving Knowledge Space.
a_rows_sample.statement: C-15 (a formal Kernel candidate about retraction) is reframed: rather than 'Knowledge can be retracted', the deeper model is 'Knowledge is always knowledge-at-a-time within an evolving Knowledge Space.' A projection is a view/selection of the evolving space at a point in time per perspective/purpose/agent/context; 'Knowledge X was true/justified at T1' does not necessarily imply 'X must remain true/usable at T2' — historical knowledge doesn't disappear, a later projection simply doesn't contain it as currently applicable.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We must **not now conclude that Projection solves C-15**. That would be jumping from brainstorming into architecture.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit governance discipline: the brainstorming Projection idea must not be treated as solving C-15, only as an alternative hypothesis — 'Maybe temporal change belongs to the relationship between Knowledge Space and Projection rather than to the epistemic state of the Knowledge object itself' — which C-15 should test, not adopt directly.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ### KnowledgeCore ... ### Projection ... ### Knowledge Space ... ### Kernel
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposed four-part separation: KnowledgeCore protects identity, justification, admissibility, epistemic history, continuity; Projection answers 'what knowledge is relevant/visible/applicable from this perspective at this time?'; Knowledge Space represents the broader evolving space in which knowledge exists and changes; Kernel protects the fundamental epistemic guarantees without becoming the entire cognitive system. Illustrated with an AI system example: 09:00 projection 'customer is eligible' vs 14:00 projection 'customer is not currently eligible' after new evidence, without erasing the 09:00 knowledge — described as closer to a 'persistent epistemic brain' than a simple CRUD knowledge base.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Absence must not silently become an epistemic state.
a_rows_sample.statement: Danger flagged in the Projection model: 'If Projection P2 doesn't contain X, therefore X is false' would be wrong, since absence from a projection could mean not relevant, not visible, not assessed, outside scope, unavailable, superseded, or genuinely no longer justified — these are different meanings. This connects to the ZERO lens: absence must not silently become an epistemic state, giving another reason to preserve ZERO discipline within the Projection idea.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The formal Kernel work is deliberately asking: **What is the smallest authoritative boundary?** Your brainstorming was asking a different question: **What kind of epistemic world would make such a Kernel useful?**
a_rows_sample.statement: Two complementary but distinct questions must not be mixed during adjudication: the formal Kernel work asks 'What is the smallest authoritative boundary?' while the brainstorming asks 'What kind of epistemic world would make such a Kernel useful?' Recommended sequence: BRAINSTORMING (Knowledge/Knowledge Space/Time/Projection/Identity/Evidence/Reasoning) -> FORMAL KERNEL (what must absolutely be protected) -> ADJUDICATION (what is actually constitutional) -> FALSIFICATION (can the broader model break the proposed minimal Kernel) -> FUTURE ARCHITECTURE -> FUTURE VISION ('brain' of an AI/computer system).

a_rows_sample.anchor: | Brainstorming hypothesis | Current law | Potential challenge |
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes producing three artifacts: (A) Current Law — what KnowledgeOS currently constitutionally says; (B) Brainstorming Conceptual Model — what has been imagined/researched as possible models; (C) Falsification Matrix — where B challenges A. Gives a worked six-row example table (e.g. 'Knowledge is time-dependent' vs 'History is forward-only' -> 'Does time belong to state or projection?'; 'Knowledge can disappear from a projection without becoming false' vs 'ZERO' -> 'Strong compatibility').

a_rows_sample.anchor: Retraction may be orthogonal to epistemic status.
a_rows_sample.statement: Evaluating a prior (unnamed) review's proposal: 'Retraction may be orthogonal to epistemic status' is assessed as a genuinely important, strong hypothesis — represented as Epistemic condition (e.g. VERIFIED) staying constant while a separate Lifecycle (e.g. ACTIVE -> RETRACTED) changes, rather than an epistemic-state transition VERIFIED->RETRACTED. This protects the distinction 'currently relied upon' != 'true' — 'we no longer rely on X' does not mean 'X is false' — assessed as one of the strongest points in the review.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "Lifecycle status already exists" is not established... It proposes four lifecycle states — that's already architecture
a_rows_sample.statement: Challenges the prior review on two counts: (1) its claim 'the Kernel already supports lifecycle transitions' is not established without checking v1.1 — a forward-only lifecycle existing is a different proposition from a separate lifecycle-state-model existing; (2) proposing four lifecycle states (PROPOSED/ACTIVE/RETRACTED/SUPERSEDED) from the orthogonality finding alone is 'architecture by inference' — the Zero lens can show retraction need not be an epistemic state, but cannot by itself justify a specific four-state machine. Separates Finding ('retraction may be orthogonal to epistemic status') from Hypothesis ('a lifecycle axis could represent that orthogonality') from Proposed architecture ('Kernel contains a four-state lifecycle model') — only the first is currently a useful finding.

a_rows_sample.anchor: who is allowed to assert the retraction? That takes us directly into: **authority, agency and decision power.**
a_rows_sample.statement: C-15 may not be merely a state-model problem but a boundary-ownership problem: when 'the organization no longer relies on K123', who decides that — KnowledgeCore, Authority, Projection, Decision Boundary, an external business context, or a governance process — and who is allowed to assert the retraction? This is an open question connecting directly to authority, agency, and decision power.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Can the lifecycle interpretation represent retraction without introducing a second hidden epistemic state machine?
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that Epistemic State + Lifecycle State could become excellent architecture or could explode into Epistemic State Machine x Lifecycle State Machine x Authority State Machine x Projection State Machine, at which point 'the small Kernel has exploded' — the ZERO lens should attack the lifecycle proposal too. Final verdict: classify the reviewed proposal as a HIGH-VALUE RESEARCH HYPOTHESIS (labeled C-15-H1: 'Retraction may be orthogonal to epistemic status and representable as lifecycle/process semantics without adding an epistemic state'), not a C-15 ruling and not an implementation instruction, to be tested against v1.1, Knowledge Space model, Projection model, Identity invariant, forward-only lifecycle, History, Agency, Authority, ZERO lens, and the minimal-boundary criterion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A decision-ready state is a Knowledge State that is sufficiently complete, coherent, and adequate for the current purpose, such that the Knower can make an informed decision with acceptable confidence.
a_rows_sample.statement: Original Q23 definition: a decision-ready state is a Knowledge State sufficiently complete, coherent and adequate for the current purpose, such that the Knower can make an informed decision with acceptable confidence. Boxed: Decision-Ready ≠ Complete; Decision-Ready = Sufficient for Purpose; Stop Condition = f(Sufficiency, Cost, Urgency, Risk, Policy).

a_rows_sample.anchor: ShouldStop(S_t, P_t, C_t, Policy_t) \in \{\text{True}, \text{False}\}
a_rows_sample.statement: The Stop Condition Framework: ShouldStop(S_t,P_t,C_t,Policy_t) is a boolean function of six criteria (Sufficiency S_u, Diminishing Returns D_r, Time/Cost T_c, Urgency U_r, Risk R_i, Policy P_o), combined as ShouldStop = Sufficient(S_t,P_t) ∨ BudgetExhausted(S_t,T_c) ∨ UrgencyThreshold(S_t,U_r) ∨ PolicyStop(S_t,P_o).

type_signature.domain: system state x purpose x context x policy

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sufficient(S_t, P_t) = \text{KnowledgeSufficient}(K_t, I^K_t) \land \text{UnderstandingSufficient}(U_t, I^U_t) \land \text{DomainSufficient}(X_t, I^D_t)
a_rows_sample.statement: Sufficiency is decomposed into Knowledge, Understanding and Domain sufficiency: Knowledge sufficient requires all ideal dimensions represented (D_I ⊆ D_Kt), all critical values known, all critical epistemic states meeting a threshold Σ_I, all critical relationships represented, and coherence maintained. Understanding sufficient requires conceptual understanding, implications understanding, uncertainty and conflict-resolution each meeting thresholds. Domain sufficient requires reality meeting constraints (X_t ⊨ C_I) and performance meeting a threshold.

a_rows_sample.anchor: \text{DiminishingReturns}(S_t) = \text{ExpectedValue}(\text{NextInvestigation}) < \text{Cost}(\text{NextInvestigation})
a_rows_sample.statement: Diminishing returns occur when the expected value of the next investigation step is less than its cost; ExpectedValue(d) = Impact(d) x Probability(d is actionable) x Severity(d); Cost(d) = Time(d) + Effort(d) + Resources(d).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Readiness = w_K \cdot K_c + w_U \cdot U_d + w_C \cdot C_r + w_{U_l} \cdot (1 - U_l) + w_D \cdot D_i + w_R \cdot R_t
a_rows_sample.statement: Original Readiness function: a weighted scalar in [0,1] over six factors (Knowledge Completeness K_c, Understanding Depth U_d, Conflict Resolution C_r, Uncertainty Level U_l, Decision Impact D_i, Risk Tolerance R_t); DecisionReady(S_t,P_t) iff Readiness(S_t,P_t) >= Threshold(P_t).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 8. The Arjuna Example: Stop Decision
a_rows_sample.statement: Walkthrough of Arjuna's decision states S0 (insufficient knowledge/understanding/domain, continue), S1 (partially sufficient after observation, continue), S2 (sufficient after moral resolution, STOP and present decision-ready state); stop criteria table shows sufficiency, diminishing returns, urgency and risk all favoring Stop.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionReady \neq ShouldStop
a_rows_sample.statement: Correction to Q23: the original equation ShouldStop = Sufficient ∨ BudgetExhausted ∨ UrgencyThreshold ∨ PolicyStop is 'too permissive' because it implies exhausting budget or reaching urgency can make a state decision-ready, which is not epistemically correct. Fundamental distinction established: DecisionReady ≠ ShouldStop, and a forced stop does not mean the system is decision-ready (Stop ⇏ DecisionReady). Three outcomes of investigation identified: Decision-Ready→STOP, Not Ready→Continue, Not Ready→Forced Stop.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Unknown \neq Not\ Decision\ Ready
a_rows_sample.statement: Correction: the requirement that all critical dimension values be 'known' is too strong — some values can remain unknown while the decision is still valid if the uncertainty is decision-irrelevant (example: not knowing whether a probability is 17% or 18% when both lead to the same decision). Replaces with DecisionRelevantUncertainty(S_t,D) ≤ T_D, a policy-defined tolerance T_D.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Case C — Decision-critical unresolved conflict
a_rows_sample.statement: Refines 'conflicts resolved or accepted' into three ConflictStatus cases: (A) Resolved; (B) Accepted as unresolved (Knower explicitly accepts the uncertainty/conflict); (C) Active and decision-critical unresolved conflict, in which case DecisionReady = False. 'Accepted' therefore cannot automatically mean readiness.

a_rows_sample.anchor:
Knowledge = 95%
Understanding = 95%
Conflict Resolution = 95%
Critical unresolved safety conflict = YES
a_rows_sample.statement: The weighted-average Readiness score assumes all dimensions are compensable: a hypothetical case with 95% knowledge/understanding/conflict-resolution but an unresolved critical safety conflict could still average to Readiness=0.9 and incorrectly declare the state decision-ready. Presented as the counterexample motivating replacement of the scalar formula.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionReady = \bigwedge_i G_i \land SoftCriteriaSatisfied
a_rows_sample.statement: Replaces the compensable weighted scalar with a hard-gates-plus-soft-indicators architecture: non-negotiable hard constraints G_1..G_n (e.g. G1=Coherent(K_t), G2=NoDecisionCriticalConflict, G3=CriticalEvidenceSatisfied, G4=CriticalDimensionsSatisfied) must all hold, DecisionReady = (⋀_i G_i) ∧ SoftCriteriaSatisfied. Readiness is redefined as a structured triple (HardGates, SoftIndicators, RemainingDeficiencies) rather than a scalar in [0,1]; a scalar R_score=f(SoftIndicators) may still be derived for UI purposes but must never override hard constraints. States the principle: 'Structured state is fundamental; scalar measurements are derived,' attributed as following from Q19/Q22.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EVSI = Expected\ Value\ of\ Information
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the diminishing-returns formula to account for decision impact via the Expected Value of Sample/Information (EVSI): EVSI(a) = E[decision quality after information] − decision quality now; continue investigation when expected decision benefit exceeds cost/risk. Flagged as an optional decision-theoretic mechanism, not a universal mathematical truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Status = ForcedStopNotReady
a_rows_sample.statement: Urgency must not produce false readiness: 'Not sufficient + Urgent = STOP' is operationally fine but must produce Status = ForcedStopNotReady, not DecisionReady = True.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Discrepancy \rightarrow Findings \rightarrow Resolution Opportunities \rightarrow Prioritization \rightarrow Investigation \rightarrow Decision Sufficiency \rightarrow Decision Posture
a_rows_sample.statement: Overall assessment gives the original Q23 scores Conceptual 8/10, Mathematical 6.5/10, DDD 7.5/10, expecting 9.5/9/9.5 after corrections. States the central architectural insight: KnowledgeOS does not decide when 'enough knowledge' exists in the abstract, but whether enough decision-relevant knowledge exists for this Knower, this purpose, this context, and this decision — giving a progression chain from Discrepancy through Findings, Resolution Opportunities, Prioritization, Investigation, Decision Sufficiency, to Decision Posture (Q19→Q22→Q23).

a_rows_sample.anchor: A decision-ready state exists before presentation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrected definition: 'A decision-ready state is an evaluated system state in which the knowledge relevant to a specific decision satisfies the applicable decision criteria. Presentation is the projection of that state into a form usable by the Knower.' Formalized as DecisionReady(S_t,D,P,C) followed by P_t = Present(DecisionReadyState, Knower, Format), preserving the Q23 distinction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Resolution \neq \Delta=\emptyset
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects the previous Arjuna example's claim 'After Moral Resolution -> Δ=∅' as a very important correction: even after normative resolution, uncertainty/risk/incomplete domain knowledge/emotional difficulty/consequences may remain, so Resolution ≠ Δ=∅; DecisionReady(Δ,P) may hold even though Δ≠∅. Generalized to abandon 'Δ=∅ ⇒ Success' entirely: DecisionReady=CriteriaSatisfied, not DecisionReady=NoRemainingGaps, so CompleteKnowledge is unnecessary for action — 'a very important property for a real engineering system'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionReady(S,C) \iff DecisionCriteria(S,C)
a_rows_sample.statement: Clarifies that 'DecisionReady does not require Δ=∅' remains architecturally correct but is the theory's own engineering inference, not a theorem Chapter 3 itself establishes: DecisionReady(S,C) ⟺ DecisionCriteria(S,C), not DecisionReady ⟺ Δ=∅ — a design principle derived from the case, not a claim about the text.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Question 20 — What is the complete system state, and how does it evolve?
a_rows_sample.statement: Fragment listing question prompts without worked answers: Q16 'How do observation, evidence, inference, contradiction, uncertainty and resolution change epistemic status?'; Q17/Q19 (duplicated) 'How do we mathematically measure the difference between K_t and the relevant Ideal State without reducing fundamentally different deficiencies to an arbitrary scalar?'; a differently-numbered 'Question 17 — How do Zero, Lord, and Sārathi interact with the transition system?'; Question 20 'What is the complete system state, and how does it evolve?'; Question 21 'How do we prioritize which deficiencies to address first?'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Status = ForcedStopNotReady
b_rows_sample.statement: Urgency must not produce false readiness: 'Not sufficient + Urgent = STOP' is operationally fine but must produce Status = ForcedStopNotReady, not DecisionReady = True.

b_rows_sample.anchor: InvestigationStatus \in \{Ready,\ Continue,\ ForcedStop,\ Unresolvable\}
b_rows_sample.statement: Recommends replacing the boolean ShouldStop with four terminal InvestigationStatus values: Decision Ready (evidence/understanding satisfy decision criteria), Continue Investigation (more investigation warranted), Forced Stop — Not Ready (must stop but readiness not achieved), Unresolvable (required knowledge cannot currently be obtained/resolved).

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'investigation-terminal-states' POSSIBLY relates to 'decision-readiness-stop-condition-model' (batch B0020). Note: Replacement for boolean ShouldStop: Ready | Continue | ForcedStop | Unresolvable, correcting the conflation of forced stopping with decision-readiness.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H. Gap impact table ... 'EvalReq has no codomain' CLOSED ... G-01 RE-SCOPED, and the count is now known: Four codomains ... NEW G-24 ... NEW G-25 ... Re-founding #6, 2026-09-06 00:23 — a 23-document, 21-part rewrite that declares it will not inherit, and cites the 025-series zero times while re-deriving its conclusions
a_rows_sample.statement: Records gap-register impact: CLOSES 'EvalReq has no codomain' (supplied at birth and by composition) and 'S_sat is undefined' (defined in theory-part-03, 9 minutes before theory-part-06 uses it); RE-SCOPES G-01 with the codomain count now known precisely as FOUR non-reconciled codomains (S 9->10->11 in 025d, V_Sat 3-valued in Sat_c, S_sat 4-valued in theory-part-03, S_sat again in theory-part-06 -- same as theory-part-03's -- with no document mapping any pair); opens NEW G-24 (V_Sat is defined, boxed and complete, yet occurs in exactly one file corpus-wide -- a codomain with zero downstream consumers); opens NEW G-25 (the 2026-09-06 00:23 re-founding itself: a 23-document, 21-part theory rewrite that explicitly declares it will not inherit prior formulations and cites the 025-series zero times while re-deriving its conclusions); leaves C-1/G-09 unchanged, untouched by this reconstruction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I. Next step, by dependency impact ... G-25 — the 2026-09-06 re-founding. ... every object this family cares about is born inside it ... every 09-06 formulation is of unknown ancestry ... G-12 remains the larger chronological debt but is not upstream of this family. Firewall honoured. Nothing canonicalized.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies G-25 (the 2026-09-06 re-founding) as the single highest-dependency-impact next research step: it is upstream of the entire 09-06 lane (23 documents, a complete rewrite, and every family object -- Det_r, S_sat, the Eval/EvalReq/Det_r decomposition -- born inside it), so until its inheritance relation to the 025-series is established, every 09-06 formulation is of unknown ancestry, and G-01/G-05/C-1/the Det_r question all have one endpoint inside it. Notes G-12 (the large chronological read-debt) remains larger in absolute scope but is NOT upstream of this particular family. Confirms firewall honoured throughout, nothing canonicalized, no definition selected, all versions preserved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §2 Corpus census — and a defect in my own first pass ... My first census reported 224 missing. A greedy regex ... Re-run with a first-match search: 3 missing, agreeing with the corpus's own four independent records.
b_rows_sample.statement: Census of the 026-268 interval: 240 distinct step numbers, 265 files, 3 genuinely missing (217, 229, 268), 21 duplicated step numbers. Reports catching its own regex defect: a greedy pattern matched the LAST 'step-' token in a filename embedding a different step number in its title, falsely reporting step 224 as missing; corrected with a first-match search to agree with the corpus's own four independent records of exactly 3 missing steps. Notes this is the second regex defect caught this week in this programme (after a missing word-boundary in the Sat birth census), both caught before entering an artifact.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §4–5 Object births ... Eight of nine objects are born in ONE MORNING — 10:14 to 12:26 on 2026-08-28, steps 026–099.
b_rows_sample.statement: Mechanically derives birth times (both Unicode and LaTeX spellings, ordered by mtime not step number) for nine major objects: Zero (08-28 10:14, s026), K_t (10:15, s028), Omega (10:22, s031, Omega:W->O SS31.18), tau (10:22, s031), EC (10:23, s032), Delta_t (10:40, s047), Gamma (11:36, s053), Req (12:26, s099), and Determination (13:44, s155a, but flagged as not a true birth). Finds eight of nine objects born within a single morning window (10:14-12:26, steps 026-099).

b_rows_sample.anchor: ⛔ Determination is not born at 155a ... Our previous architecture identified Determination. I would now make its semantics explicit. ⇒ RECONSTRUCTION ONLY / retrospective import ... Compare Det_r ... Strong structural similarity, zero citation ⇒ IDENTITY UNWITNESSED.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Determination's apparent 155a birth: the source itself says 'our previous architecture identified Determination; I would now make its semantics explicit', classifying this as RECONSTRUCTION ONLY / retrospective import, not a true concept birth -- the corpus-wide earliest occurrence is actually in reviews/ (2026-08-19 00:57), a governance lane, nine days earlier. Records 155a's formalization Determination=f(Claim,Evidence,Method,Context) with f unnamed and no codomain, plus Evidence!=Determination and Verification subset-of Determination. Compares this to Det_r:VxEC->S_sat (born 09-06): 155a carries the 'how' as an explicit Method argument while Det_r carries it as a function-name index plus EC -- strong structural similarity but zero citation between them, classified IDENTITY UNWITNESSED.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The silences are the structure ... The interval is not gradual evolution. It is: everything introduced in one morning, then 100–157 files of near-total silence, then a return in the 183–267 band. ... The terminal staircase ... they die one per step, at the very end
b_rows_sample.statement: Measures each object's longest silence gap in files: Gamma 157 files (s053->s197), Omega 155 files (s031->s186-pre), EC 135 (s117->s238), Delta_t 117 (s047->s155a), tau 112 (s074->s188), Zero 74 (s094->recovery doc). Concludes the interval's shape is NOT gradual evolution but a sharp pattern: everything introduced in one morning, then a 100-157 file near-total silence, then a return in the 183-267 band. Also finds a 'terminal staircase' where nine objects die one per step in sequence near the end of the interval (Req s234, Delta_t s240, EC s251, Determination s252, tau s263, Zero s264, K_t s265, Omega s266, Gamma s267).

b_rows_sample.anchor: §16 Q1 · What happened to the 025-series apparatus? ... The 025 apparatus enters the interval EXACTLY ONCE — at step 251, two days later, as a HISTORICAL TABLE ROW. Never as a live formulation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Censuses eight 025-series objects (Derive(H,Omega,EC), R_G, Gamma_G, EC_G, ContractSpecific, EpistemicContract, Sat/Satisfied/Sat_c, EvalReq/EvalRequirement) across all 265 interval files and finds zero occurrences of every named component except a bare 'Satisfied' word (2 hits) and Update(K_t,E_t,Omega,EC) appearing exactly once, at step_251, inside a historical genealogy table; '025' is cited by name exactly once in 265 files (also step_251), with an apparent second citation at step-152 identified and discarded as a false positive (a constitution clause number 'C-025'). Concludes the entire 025 apparatus enters the interval exactly once, two days later, as a historical table row, never as a live formulation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: And yet continuity was declared, 41 seconds later ... step-025z ... 2026-08-28 10:13:25 ... step-026 ... 41 seconds later ... 'We continue from 25Z.' ... Continuity is DECLARED by name, 41 seconds later — and the apparatus is not CARRIED. Declaration ≠ transmission.
b_rows_sample.statement: Finds the last 025-series document (step-025z) was written 2026-08-28 10:13:25, and step-026 was written just 41 seconds later, with step-026's third line explicitly stating 'We continue from 25Z.' Concludes continuity is declared by name almost immediately, yet none of the 025 apparatus is actually carried forward -- establishing the general principle that declaration does not equal transmission. Notes in passing a step-number homonym found incidentally: a different, unrelated step-026 document exists dated 2026-08-27 16:29:19 (a work-programme document), one day earlier, same step number, unrelated content.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §12–13 · The re-founding hypothesis — tested on all six candidates ... NOT ONE DECLARES A RESTART. Every discontinuity in this corpus is MEASURED, never DECLARED.
b_rows_sample.statement: Tests all six previously-labeled re-founding candidates against their own opening words: 026 ('we continue from 25Z') = CONTINUITY DECLARED; 031 ('step 31 is the first deliberate attempt to turn that architecture into a formal system') = CONTINUITY, a MODE CHANGE not a restart; 183-pre ('substantially aligned... but some later formulations should NOT be promoted') = SELECTIVE REJECTION of a named subset; 186-pre ('construct the mathematics around the distinctions we have already established') = CONTINUITY; 230 ('determine whether the apparently large architecture can be generated from a small kernel') = REDUCTION of the existing architecture; 262 ('we can now continue, but there is an important correction to the previous Step 261 conclusion') = CORRECTION; and the 09-06 rewrite (via G-25) = SELECTIVE INHERITANCE. Concludes not one of the six candidates declares a restart -- every discontinuity in this corpus is measured (by an outside investigator finding lost apparatus) rather than declared (by the author announcing a break).

b_rows_sample.anchor: ⛔ WITHDRAWAL — the 'five re-foundings' record ... G-25 already removed the sixth. This reconstruction removes the concept. ... apparatus is lost across declared continuities. Authors say they continue, and mean it; the objects do not travel with the declaration.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally withdraws the corpus's own '07-THEORYSTATE-CHRONICLE.md' record of five re-foundings (031, 183-pre, 230, 262, 273), revising each label: 031's 'INDEPENDENT_REFOUNDING (drops the 025 apparatus)' is corrected -- 031 itself says it continues Steps 1-30; it is actually 026 that drops the apparatus while declaring continuity, the opposite framing; 183-pre's 'EXPLICIT_REPLACEMENT (pruning)' is downgraded to SELECTIVE_REJECTION since it affirms alignment and rejects only a named subset; 230's 'UNWITNESSED' becomes REDUCTION since it explicitly presupposes the existing architecture; 262's 'EXPLICIT_REPLACEMENT' becomes CORRECTION since it names its predecessor and corrects one specific conclusion; 273 unchanged. Concludes (with G-25 having already removed the sixth candidate) this reconstruction removes the whole 're-founding' CONCEPT itself, replacing five separate events with one general mechanism: in this corpus, apparatus is lost across declared continuities -- authors say they continue and mean it, but the objects do not travel with the declaration.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §8 · Mathematical audit — Update, the interval's most overloaded operation ... Ten distinct signatures for one operation name, none related to any other. Arity 2–4, each in 1–3 files, zero cross-references. ⇒ IDENTITY UNWITNESSED at scale.
b_rows_sample.statement: Finds ten distinct Update(...) signatures in the interval (arities 2-4: Update(K_t,E_t,Omega,EC), Update(K,E), Update(K_t,E_{t+1}), Update(K_t,V_{t+1},Delta_t), Update(K_t,O_{t+1}), Update(K_t,E_t), Update(K_t,E_new), Update(K,y), Update(K_t,V,G), Update(K_t,Outcome_I)), each occurring in only 1-3 files with zero cross-references between them, classified IDENTITY UNWITNESSED at scale. Independently corroborated by the master gap register's G-16 finding of '45 distinct RHS strings, 11 named transition functions, arities 1-6, no settled signature.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: The codomain defect is inherited across three eras ... Status ... Determination = f(Claim,Evidence,Method,Context) ... none ... EvalReq(K,r,EC,Γ) ... none ... Three objects, three eras, three lanes — the same defect, never noticed by any of them.
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies a single recurring defect across three unrelated objects, eras and lanes: Status (025e, 08-27) is named but never defined; Determination=f(Claim,Evidence,Method,Context) (155a, 08-28) has no codomain at all; EvalReq(K,r,EC,Gamma) (theory-part-06, 09-06) has no codomain (V is only type-constrained, never stated). Concludes this identical defect recurs across three separate objects, eras and lanes, never noticed by any of them independently -- generalizing the earlier per-object findings into a single corpus-wide pattern.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §16 · The ten questions Q1–Q10 (full table)
b_rows_sample.statement: Answers ten structured research questions about the interval: Q1 the 025 apparatus did not cross (0 in 265 files, cited once as a table row 41 seconds after continuity was declared); Q2 Omega/tau/K_t/Zero/EC/Delta_t/Gamma/Req are all born inside the interval (inherited from nothing) while Determination is genuinely inherited from a governance lane; Q3 the whole evaluation/satisfaction family was independently re-derived, clearest case Determination's 155a formalization vs Det_r; Q4 no definition inside the interval completes an earlier one -- all distributed-completeness successes cross OUT of the interval; Q5 apparent gaps (Omega:W->O, EvalReq's codomain-name, S_sat) were all resolved from OUTSIDE the interval; Q6 genuine type changes found in Update (10 signatures), Omega (5 senses), Sat (4 codomains); Q7 homonyms/identity-unwitnessed cases include Omega x5, Update x10, Gamma, Determination (governance vs mathematical), and step-026 itself (two documents, one number, a day apart); Q8 K-formulation origins traced (K_t s028; K_v1 7-tuple at 031; K_v2 6-tuple only in an s155-156 recovery doc quoting 'the earlier model'; K_v3 (A,R) from outside the interval); Q9 per-object silence/activity counts (Sat and EvalReq: ZERO occurrences in the entire interval); Q10 three carry-forward lessons: declared continuity != transmitted apparatus, the terminal staircase pattern, and the inherited codomain defect across three eras.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §18 · Terminal classification (Ω class E, Sat/EvalReq class C, Determination class E, Update class E, K_t class B, the interval itself class A structural)
b_rows_sample.statement: Issues terminal classifications: Omega = class E (OBJECT IDENTITY UNRESOLVED, five senses, 0 of 10 pairs same, per G-22); Sat/EvalReq = class C (COMPETING COMPLETE DEFINITIONS, four codomains, two indexing strategies, per G-25, though entirely absent from this interval); Determination = class E (IDENTITY UNRESOLVED across governance birth, mathematical formalization, and Det_r, no citation between any pair); Update/transition = class E (10 signatures, no stated relation); K_t = class B (complete through multiple sources, but those sources are outside the interval); the interval itself = class A, COMPLETE HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION (structural) -- births, silences, returns and deaths now fully mapped mechanically for 9 objects over 265 files.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §14 · Negative history ... Not found: Sat, Sat_c, EvalReq, EvalRequirement, R_G, Γ_G, EC_G, Derive(H,Ω,EC), ContractSpecific, EpistemicContract. ⇒ Recorded DEFINED ELSEWHERE ... not GENUINE CORPUS GAP. Det_r's body remains FIREWALL-LIMITED
b_rows_sample.statement: Reports a negative-history search across all 265 files (both spellings, word-bounded, first-match step extraction) confirming zero occurrences of ten named objects (Sat, Sat_c, EvalReq, EvalRequirement, R_G, Gamma_G, EC_G, Derive(H,Omega,EC), ContractSpecific, EpistemicContract). Correctly classifies these as DEFINED ELSEWHERE (they exist before the interval at 023/025 and after it at 09-02/09-06) rather than GENUINE CORPUS GAP, per the programme's own discipline against declaring absence-within-a-bounded-window a true gap. Det_r's body remains classified FIREWALL-LIMITED (97% of occurrences excluded). Confirms firewall honoured, nothing canonicalized, no definition selected, all versions preserved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §12 · Continuity with apparatus loss — the Ω instance, and it is sharper than 026's ... A gap was opened for an object the corpus had DEFINED THREE DAYS EARLIER — and then closed by 'recovering' it. ... apparatus never left the corpus — only the working set — and its re-discovery was recorded as a gap closure.
b_rows_sample.statement: Traces a precise sequence: 031 defines Omega:W->O boxed (08-28 10:22) -> a 155-file silence -> Omega returns (08-29) -> step_251 cites it unattributed (08-30) -> a NEW GAP is explicitly opened ('Gap 1: (W,Omega) referent layer', 08-31 19:03) -> the same gap is closed hours later by 'recovering' the Sanjaya layer (08-31 19:52, G3->G5) -> a claim that 'the earlier claim that the verification lane lacked an entire observation/referent layer is no longer valid' (08-31 19:40) -> Omega-A's document frames this as resolving 'a structural omission discovered in D285-6' (08-31 20:11). Concludes a gap was opened for an object the corpus had already defined three days earlier, then closed by 'recovering' it -- the corpus does not record this as a loss, it records it as a discovery. Contrasts this with G-12's 026 mechanism ('continuity declared, apparatus not carried'): here, the apparatus never left the corpus at all, only the ACTIVE WORKING SET did, and its re-discovery was mislabeled a gap closure -- two distinct mechanisms in one family, recorded as evidence not generalized into a law.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §1–4 · The 025→026 boundary, object by object — and my G-12 headline qualified ... The concepts did not stop. They de-formalised. ... sufficiency 73% ... satisfaction 45% ... contract 40% ... The NOTATION was lost. The CONCEPTS ran on through 45–73% of the interval.
b_rows_sample.statement: Qualifies the prior G-12 finding that the 025 apparatus 'vanishes' at step 026: while all formal 025 SYMBOLS score exactly 0 across 265 files (confirmed true), a census of the underlying 025-era CONCEPTS in prose form finds sufficiency at 73% (193/265 files), satisfaction at 45% (120/265), contract at 40% (107/265), gap at 20%, acceptance criterion at 2%, while the specific phrase 'requirement evaluation' scores 0. Concludes the NOTATION was lost but the CONCEPTS ran on informally through 45-73% of the interval -- the earlier headline ('the apparatus vanishes') is true only of formal notation, not of underlying concepts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: And precisely which form survived ... Of 241 satisf* occurrences sampled: 83 in technical context, 158 prose. ... What survived is satisfaction as a PREDICATE. What was lost is satisfaction as a TYPED FUNCTION WITH A RESULT SPACE.
b_rows_sample.statement: Samples 241 'satisf*' occurrences (83 technical, 158 prose) and verifies at ten specific steps (s070,079,081,086,091,092,095,097,098,101) that the surviving technical usage is uniformly an unformalised predicate ('the rule is satisfied', 'invariants remain satisfied') rather than the 025-series typed function Satisfied(K,r,EC) with three typed arguments and a result space S(9->10->11). Concludes precisely what survived was satisfaction AS A PREDICATE; what was lost was satisfaction as a TYPED FUNCTION WITH A RESULT SPACE.

b_rows_sample.anchor: An interpretation, marked as such ... consistent with — and would explain — the four divergent Sat codomains found in G-25 ... nothing carried a result space through the interval, so each later lane supplied its own. ⛔ Recorded as [PROPOSED], not as a cause.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes, explicitly marked as an unproven interpretation (not a corpus-stated cause), that the loss of a shared result space during the interval would explain why G-25 later found four mutually non-citing Sat codomains (S 9-11, V_Sat 3, S_sat 4, S_sat variant): each later lane, lacking an inherited result space, supplied its own. Notes this hypothesis is recorded as [PROPOSED] rather than established, citing a cautionary precedent -- a previously withdrawn batch-003 claim ('the semantics-bearing argument always disappears') that failed for exactly the same overreach.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §6 · Distributed completeness — the corrected classification ... EvalReq is the only 025-era object whose concept as well as its notation leaves the interval. That singles it out, and it is the one object G-25 found still untyped at 09-06.
b_rows_sample.statement: Provides a corrected four-row classification: '025 apparatus vanishes at 026' is corrected from PARTIALLY-EVIDENCED to DE-FORMALISED (symbols 0, concepts 45-73%); 'Sat is absent from 026-268' stands for the FUNCTION but is FALSE for the underlying CONCEPT (0 vs 120 files); 'EvalReq is absent' stands fully, both notation and concept (even the phrase 'requirement evaluation' scores 0/265); 'Omega-B has no type' is REFUTED (excluded by design, per S14). Concludes EvalReq is uniquely the only 025-era object whose CONCEPT, not merely its notation, actually leaves the interval -- and it is the same object G-25 separately found still untyped as late as 09-06.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §8, §12 · Identity and DDD — EC is the interval's worst case ... Three ECs, three arities, three bounded contexts, zero cross-references ... Verdict: HOMONYM ×3, IDENTITY UNWITNESSED between every pair.
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies EC as a triple homonym with zero cross-references between any pair: EC=EpistemicClaim (s032, 11-tuple, 'the atomic unit of KnowledgeOS'); EC=engineering change (s117, 8-tuple, 'a test object' in a traceability experiment); EC=EpistemicContract (025-series, (R_G,Gamma_G) shape, 0 occurrences in steps 026-154). Classifies this as HOMONYM x3 with IDENTITY UNWITNESSED between every pair, noting it is the same shape of finding as Determination (governance vs mathematical vs Det_r) and Gamma (four senses), already recorded elsewhere in this programme.

b_rows_sample.anchor: §7 · Mathematical typing across the interval (PROVEN: Ω-2, K_v0, K_v1, EC-claim, Γ_A, EC-engchange; UNKNOWN: Zero never defined, Δ_t only α_t defined, Ω_t unresolved, Update 10 signatures) ... No promotion of TYPE-CONSTRAINED or INFERRED to PROVEN.
b_rows_sample.statement: Audits mathematical typing status across the interval: PROVEN objects include Omega-2 (W->O), K_v0 (9-tuple, s028), K_v1 (7-tuple, s031), EC-claim (11-tuple, s032), Gamma_A (4-tuple, s053), EC-engchange (8-tuple, s117); UNKNOWN status objects include Zero (never defined anywhere in 265 files), Delta_t (one occurrence, whose 'where' clause defines only a sub-component alpha_t, not Delta_t itself), Omega_t as an argument of delta_K (signature declared unresolved by its own cited sources), and Update (10 unrelated signatures). Notes no TYPE-CONSTRAINED or INFERRED-status object was promoted to PROVEN in this pass.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 24 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: Arjuna does not need to know what a dimension is... ObserverIntent \neq DimensionSpecification
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes that the Knower's natural-language intent is not itself a dimension specification; KnowledgeOS/Sarathi performs Analyze(Q0,CurrentState,Context) -> CandidateDimensions, so the observer expresses need while the system reconstructs the dimensional schema.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DimensionDiscovery(Q,K,C) \rightarrow D_{candidate} ... Observation \rightarrow D_{new} ... The two are different.
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces Dimension Discovery as a working capability (not yet a domain object) distinct from Observation-driven dimension revelation: DimensionDiscovery(Q,K,C)->D_candidate happens before/independent of Observation->D_new; three sources are named: question-derived (D_Q), observation-derived (D_O), and horizon-derived via Lord (D_L), unioned as D_investigation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS should generate candidate dimensions, not immediately declare every generated candidate to be a dimension of the observed state.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the naive Union(D_Q,...,D_Pattern)-as-dimensions model: the union is only a candidate set D^candidate_t; KnowledgeOS must run a separate DimensionAssessment step producing D^adopted, distinguishing CandidateDimension, RelevantDimension, and ObservedDimension as three concepts that must not be collapsed (guards against hallucinated dimensions).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Pattern -> Candidate, not Pattern -> Fact ... it must still be assessed in the current observation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Treats pattern-derived candidate dimensions (D_Pattern, e.g. 'dependency relationships are frequently relevant in migrations') as a learning mechanism generating candidates only, never directly as established fact -- another Zero-style safeguard against premature reification.

a_rows_sample.anchor: When does a candidate dimension become an accepted dimension of the current observation/knowledge state? ... Question 2B — When does a candidate dimension become a dimension of the knowledge state?
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses Question 2B: the boundary between Dimension Discovery and Knowledge, i.e. under what dimension-status values (UNKNOWN/RELEVANT/OBSERVED/INFERRED/ACCEPTED/REJECTED/NOT_APPLICABLE) a candidate dimension is promoted to an accepted dimension of the knowledge state, deferred ahead of Question 3 (Statement).

a_rows_sample.anchor: DimensionDiscovery is recursive. The system does not parse the initial question once and finish. It continually reconstructs the semantic space as the investigation develops.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues Dimension Discovery must be recursive: a new question Q1 generated from prior discoveries re-enters the language-analysis pipeline (Q1 -> SemanticStructure1 -> D2), linking language analysis to the earlier progressive-investigation levels concretely (Level 0 initial parse, Level 1 relationship discovery, Level 2 duty/obligation, Level 3 consequence dimensions).

a_rows_sample.anchor: The Sanskrit grammar lens is an analytical lens from which KnowledgeOS may learn useful principles of semantic decomposition. It is not evidence that the KnowledgeOS ontology must conform to Sanskrit grammar... Likewise: The Gita is not proof of our mathematical model.
a_rows_sample.statement: States an explicit methodological discipline: neither the Sanskrit grammar lens nor the Gita narrative is evidence that KnowledgeOS's ontology must conform to them -- both are sources from which useful structural/semantic principles may be observed and tested, not authoritative specifications.

a_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal P : \mathcal L \rightarrow \mathcal S ... \mathcal D : (\mathcal S, \mathcal C, \mathcal K) \rightarrow 2^{\mathcal D_{candidate}} ... D_{candidate} = Union(D_Q, D_C, D_{Domain}, D_{Pattern}, D_{Zero}, D_{Lord})
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives the batch's most complete formal signatures: a parser P:L->S (with substructural P_struct:L->T and P_sem:L->R), and Dimension Discovery D:(S,C,K)->2^{D_candidate} with the union formula over six named sources, plus a pseudocode algorithm.

a_rows_sample.anchor: D_{t+1} = \mathcal D(\mathcal P(Q_t), K_t, C_t) ... Discovery terminates when: Z(K_t) = \emptyset or DecisionSufficiency(K_t,I_t) = True
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the recursive discovery/investigation/question-generation cycle (Q_t -parse-> S_t -discover-> D_{t+1} -investigate-> K_{t+1} -Zero+Lord-> Q_{t+1}) together with an explicit termination condition: discovery stops when Zero finds no more gaps or decision sufficiency is reached relative to the Ideal state I_t.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS should own the semantic reconstruction capability, while individual parsing technologies remain replaceable implementation mechanisms ... KnowledgeOS \supset Semantic\ Reconstruction \supset Parsing
a_rows_sample.statement: Decides Semantic Reconstruction is a native KnowledgeOS capability while individual parser technologies (C-type, Sanskrit-type, future LLM-based) are replaceable implementations beneath it: KnowledgeOS superset-of SemanticReconstruction superset-of Parsing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The domain capability owns the contract; parsing technologies implement the contract... The architecture should depend on SemanticRepresentation, not CParser or SanskritParser.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies a DDD dependency-inversion rule to the parsing question: architecture depends on the SemanticRepresentation contract, never on a specific parser technology; C/Sanskrit parsers become adapters/lenses that implement the contract, not fundamental domain objects.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS should not say: 'Our parser is Sanskrit grammar.' Instead: 'KnowledgeOS requires semantic-role reconstruction; Sanskrit grammar provides one important lens from which we can derive and test the required semantic capabilities.'
a_rows_sample.statement: Protects the Sanskrit-lens research from over-commitment: it must remain a learning source for deriving/testing semantic capabilities, never an architectural claim that the parser literally is Sanskrit grammar; parser physical placement (in-process/service/library) is explicitly deferred as an infrastructure decision, not an architectural one.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS = SemanticReconstruction + DimensionDiscovery + EpistemicOperations + KnowledgeModel ... Parser \in Implementation of SemanticReconstruction
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the four-part KnowledgeOS capability sum (SemanticReconstruction + DimensionDiscovery + EpistemicOperations + KnowledgeModel) with a full layered-architecture diagram, and states the final invariant KnowledgeOS != Parser, Parser subset-of KnowledgeOS's Implementation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Why Parsing Engines Must Be Replaceable: Reason 1: Technological Evolution... Reason 2: Domain Adaptation... Reason 3: Research and Learning
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives three reasons parser implementations must remain replaceable: technology evolves (C/Sanskrit-style parsers today, LLM/neural parsers tomorrow), different domains need different specialized parsers (software vs legal vs medical), and the project must be able to learn from multiple grammatical/linguistic traditions without permanent dependency on any one.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS \leftarrow LearnFrom(Sanskrit Grammar) ... KnowledgeOS \neq Implement(Sanskrit Grammar)
a_rows_sample.statement: States the 'Learning Principle': KnowledgeOS learns architectural insight from Sanskrit grammar without implementing/adopting it as the domain ontology.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Intent \rightarrow Structural\ Analysis \rightarrow Semantic\ Reconstruction \rightarrow Context\ Interpretation \rightarrow Domain\ Model \rightarrow Candidate\ Dimensions \rightarrow Observation \rightarrow Dimension\ Discovery
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects 'Question -> DimensionDiscovery' to a longer pipeline: Intent -> Structural Analysis -> Semantic Reconstruction -> Context Interpretation -> Domain Model -> Candidate Dimensions -> Observation -> Dimension Discovery, establishing Parsing ≠ DimensionDiscovery (parsing is an input capability to it). Also renames the earlier C-type/Sanskrit-grammar parser pair as Structural Language Analysis (Parser_S(Q)->SyntaxStructure) and Semantic Reconstruction (Parser_M(Q,C)->SemanticStructure), with DimensionDiscovery = f(Syntax, Semantics, Context, Domain, Knowledge); clarifies the 'Sanskrit lens' is not literal Sanskrit-grammar implementation but the requirement that natural language be reconstructed into semantic roles/relations, not merely syntactically parsed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The kernel does not merely ask: How much knowledge do I have? It first determines: Along which dimensions should this knowledge be understood? ... D_t = {d_1,...,d_{n_t}} ... n_t != n_{t+1}. ... knowledge growth is not only movement within a fixed space; it can involve discovering new dimensions of the space.
a_rows_sample.statement: At each time t the kernel first determines along which dimensions knowledge should be understood, not merely how much it has: D_t={d_1,...,d_{n_t}}, with the number of dimensions itself able to change (n_t != n_{t+1}). Knowledge purification can therefore be D_t->D_{t+1} as well as K_t->K_{t+1}: knowledge growth is not only movement within a fixed space but can involve discovering new dimensions of the space.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A dimension should not merely be a field. D_i = an independently discriminable aspect of the knowledge state. For example D_t={Version,Availability,Security,Backup,Network,Ownership}. K_t={Version=3.69,Availability=99.2%,Security=?,Backup=Valid,Network=Unknown,Ownership=TeamA}. '?' does not necessarily mean the dimension doesn't exist. It means D_i in D_t and v_i(t)=Unknown. That is different from D_i notin D_t.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a dimension formally as 'an independently discriminable aspect of the knowledge state,' illustrated with a six-dimension worked example (Version, Availability, Security, Backup, Network, Ownership) with mixed known/unknown values, establishing that an unknown-valued '?' entry means D_i in D_t and v_i(t)=Unknown -- categorically different from the dimension simply not being in D_t.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Known dimension, unknown value: P(expiry date|O). This is ordinary uncertainty about a known dimension. Unknown dimension: P(additional relevant dimension exists|O). This is uncertainty about the structure of the knowledge space. ... your point is primarily about the second one.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes two fundamentally different uncertainties: (1) known dimension, unknown value -- e.g. we know certificate expiry is relevant but not its date, P(expiry date|O), ordinary uncertainty about a known dimension; and (2) unknown dimension -- we don't know whether some additional dependency is relevant at all, P(additional relevant dimension exists|O), uncertainty about the structure of the knowledge space itself. Example: known dimensions (version, CPU, memory, repositories, network) may be well understood while other potential dimensions (identity integration, backup dependency, certificate dependency, licensing, external services, disaster recovery, operational dependency) remain undiscovered as even being relevant.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Person A knows 5 dimensions extremely well. Person B knows 20 dimensions reasonably well. ... B may have more knowledge because B has discovered a larger part of the relevant state space. ... Person C knows 5 dimensions extremely well and knows that there may be many undiscovered dimensions. Person C has less confidence in completeness, but arguably better epistemic awareness.
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows why more information does not automatically mean more knowledge: Person A knows 5 dimensions extremely precisely; Person B knows 20 dimensions reasonably well and may have more knowledge overall by having discovered more of the relevant state space despite less precision per dimension; Person C knows 5 dimensions extremely well AND knows that many dimensions may remain undiscovered -- Person C has lower completeness confidence but arguably better epistemic awareness than either A or B.

b_rows_sample.anchor: "I think my knowledge is 95%." you may mean: P(we have identified the relevant dimensions sufficiently) approx 0.95. Not: P(each fact is correct)=0.95. ... Dimension coverage: 95%. Information accuracy: 99%. Reasoning confidence: 90%. These are three different epistemic properties.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the interpretation of a stated confidence like '95% knowledge': it likely means P(we have identified the relevant dimensions sufficiently) approx 0.95, not P(each fact is correct)=0.95 -- these are completely different quantities. Separates three distinct epistemic properties that a single percentage conflates: dimension coverage (e.g. 95%), information accuracy (e.g. 99%), and reasoning confidence (e.g. 90%).

b_rows_sample.anchor: D_t = relevant dimensions of the ideal state at time t. We don't know D_t completely. We have discovered: hat-D_t subset D_t. ... D_t -> hat-D_t: Which dimensions exist/relevant? and: I_t(hat-D_t) -> K_t: What do we know about those dimensions? The first is the dimension-discovery problem. The second is the state-extraction problem.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes D_t as the relevant dimensions of the ideal state at time t (not fully known), with hat-D_t subset D_t as the discovered subset, and observed information O_t(hat-D_t) about discovered dimensions; splits the problem into two: D_t -> hat-D_t (the dimension-discovery problem: which dimensions exist/are relevant) and I_t(hat-D_t) -> K_t (the state-extraction problem: what do we know about those dimensions).

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(D_t, I_t | O_{<=t}) is much closer to what you are describing than simply: P(F|O). We should not yet assume this exact mathematical formulation is correct. It is a research hypothesis.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes P(D_t,I_t|O_{<=t}) -- joint uncertainty over the dimension set AND the values within discovered dimensions -- as a richer formulation than the simple P(F|O), explicitly flagged as a research hypothesis not yet assumed correct.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS cannot only store: "What do we know?" It must somehow preserve: "What dimensions of the subject do we currently believe are relevant?" and "How confident are we that our dimensional model is complete enough?" ... KnowledgeOS should potentially be able to say: "We have strong evidence concerning these dimensions, but there is unresolved uncertainty about whether additional relevant dimensions exist." That is a much more honest representation of knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS cannot only store 'what do we know' -- it must also preserve which dimensions are currently believed relevant and how confident the system is that its dimensional model is complete enough; without this, an AI could falsely claim 'I know everything about Nexus' when it has only modeled a handful of dimensions well. KnowledgeOS should instead be able to honestly say it has strong evidence on known dimensions but unresolved uncertainty about whether additional relevant dimensions exist.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Uncertainty begins not only when we don't know the value of something. It begins earlier -- when we don't know what things or dimensions are relevant to know about. ... Knowledge completeness = dimension coverage + information completeness within those dimensions, with uncertainty potentially existing at both levels.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the key insight simply: uncertainty begins not only when we don't know the value of something, but earlier -- when we don't know what dimensions are relevant to know about at all; therefore Knowledge completeness = dimension coverage + information completeness within those dimensions, with uncertainty potentially existing at both levels.

b_rows_sample.anchor: whether "dimension" is the right primitive at all, or whether what you are describing is more fundamentally a space of possible questions/propositions about the ideal state. That distinction could be decisive for the eventual mathematical model.
b_rows_sample.statement: Raises an open question that could be decisive for the eventual mathematical model: whether 'dimension' is the right primitive at all for this analysis, or whether what is being described is more fundamentally a space of possible questions/propositions about the ideal state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Few dimensions known / Many dimensions known x Little information per dimension / A lot of information per dimension -- Very low knowledge / Low-medium knowledge / Medium knowledge / High knowledge. But there is a crucial fifth question: How confident are we that we have discovered most of the relevant dimensions? So Knowledge may involve: Dimension Coverage x Information Quality x Determination Quality.
b_rows_sample.statement: Presents a 2x2 knowledge matrix crossing dimension count (few/many known) against information quality (little/a lot per dimension), yielding four qualitative knowledge levels (very low, low/medium, medium, high); adds a crucial fifth question -- confidence that most relevant dimensions have been discovered -- proposing conceptually (not yet as a formula) that Knowledge involves Dimension Coverage x Information Quality x Determination Quality.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Team A knows version, CPU, RAM with extremely accurate information. Team B knows version, CPU, RAM, network, dependencies, certificates, backup, authentication, monitoring, licensing, but some of their information is uncertain. It is entirely possible that: Knowledge(B) > Knowledge(A) ... Because Team B has broader dimension coverage.
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: Team A knows only version/CPU/RAM but with extremely accurate information; Team B knows ten dimensions (version, CPU, RAM, network, dependencies, certificates, backup, authentication, monitoring, licensing) but some information is uncertain; despite Team A's higher per-dimension accuracy, Knowledge(B) > Knowledge(A) is entirely possible because Team B has broader dimension coverage.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Team A says: "We know 95% of the system." Team B says: "We know 70% of the system." But Team B has discovered that there may be unknown dimensions. ... Team B may actually possess better epistemic knowledge, because it knows what it does not know. ... known unknowns vs. unknown unknowns. But your formulation is more precise because you're talking about dimensions of the ideal state, not merely missing facts.
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends the Team A/B example to a harder case: Team A claims 95% completeness with high confidence but low awareness of unknown dimensions, Team B claims only 70% completeness but has high awareness that unknown dimensions may exist; Team B may possess better epistemic knowledge because it knows what it does not know. Connects this to the known-unknowns/unknown-unknowns concept, but notes the present formulation is more precise since it concerns dimensions of the ideal state specifically, not merely missing facts in general.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A KnowledgeOS containing 10 million facts doesn't necessarily have more knowledge than one containing 1 million facts. ... Knowledge != Quantity of Information. Instead, at minimum: Knowledge ~ coverage of relevant dimensions + quality of information + confidence in completeness. Again, this is a research hypothesis, not yet a mathematical definition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues Knowledge cannot simply be measured by amount of stored information: a KnowledgeOS with 10 million facts about five dimensions need not have more knowledge than one with 1 million facts covering fifty dimensions -- Knowledge != Quantity of Information; instead, at minimum, Knowledge ~ coverage of relevant dimensions + quality of information + confidence in completeness, explicitly a research hypothesis, not yet a mathematical definition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Level 1 -- Value uncertainty: Is the installed version 2.69 or 2.70? P(X=2.69|O). Level 2 -- Structural/dimensional uncertainty: Have we identified all relevant aspects of the system? P(dimension coverage is complete|O). The second is much harder. And this is precisely where I would now be very careful about saying "measure theory solves it." ... we first need to establish what the random object actually is.
b_rows_sample.statement: Splits probability into two levels: Level 1, value uncertainty (e.g. P(X=2.69|O) -- is the installed version 2.69 or 2.70), and Level 2, structural/dimensional uncertainty (P(dimension coverage is complete|O) -- have all relevant aspects of the system been identified), the second being much harder; warns against casually claiming 'measure theory solves it' for Level 2 before establishing what the underlying random object actually is.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the observer may also need to estimate: D the space of dimensions in which that state should be described. So the problem becomes: First discover the relevant state space and then: Estimate the state within that space. ... Now we may need: P(D,X|O) where D=what dimensions are relevant; X=what values those dimensions have.
b_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes P(X|O) to P(D,X|O): an observer must jointly estimate the relevant dimension space D and the values X within it, not merely X alone -- first discover the relevant state space, then estimate the state within that space -- a much richer epistemic problem than previously formulated.

b_rows_sample.anchor: C_fact: confidence that a particular determination is correct. C_coverage: confidence that we have identified the relevant dimensions. C_model: confidence that our model of how those dimensions relate is correct. These are three different uncertainties.
b_rows_sample.statement: Separates three distinct confidence types that a single '90-95%' figure conflates: C_fact (confidence a particular determination is correct), C_coverage (confidence the relevant dimensions have been identified), and C_model (confidence the model of how those dimensions relate is correct).

b_rows_sample.anchor: IDEAL STATE -> (potentially many/infinite dimensions) -> Dimension discovery -> Which dimensions do we believe are relevant? -> State extraction -> What is the value/state of each known dimension? -> Determination -> KNOWLEDGE. And probability may potentially operate at both discovery and extraction levels.
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives a pipeline diagram: IDEAL STATE (potentially many/infinite dimensions) -> Dimension discovery (which dimensions do we believe are relevant?) -> State extraction (what is the value/state of each known dimension?) -> Determination -> KNOWLEDGE; probability may operate at both the discovery and the extraction levels.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Not simply: "How accurately can we determine the state?" but: "How do we determine both the relevant dimensions of an ideal state and the state of those dimensions, given limited observation and reasoning capacity?" ... Dimension uncertainty + Value uncertainty + Temporal change + Comparative determination -- before we make any claim about what the KnowledgeOS Kernel must contain.
b_rows_sample.statement: Revises the central research question from 'how accurately can we determine the state?' to 'how do we determine both the relevant dimensions of an ideal state and the state of those dimensions, given limited observation and reasoning capacity?'; sets the research concentration as Dimension uncertainty + Value uncertainty + Temporal change + Comparative determination, explicitly before any claim about what the KnowledgeOS Kernel must contain.

b_rows_sample.anchor: C_value: How confident are we about the values of known dimensions? C_coverage: How confident are we that we have identified the relevant dimensions? C_model: How confident are we that our model of relationships between those dimensions is correct? This suggests that "knowledge completeness" is not one number. It may be multidimensional.
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates dimension completeness as the newest and perhaps most important addition, formalizing three confidences C_value (values of known dimensions), C_coverage (identification of relevant dimensions), and C_model (correctness of the model of relationships between dimensions); suggests 'knowledge completeness' is not one number but potentially multidimensional -- a major insight, still a hypothesis.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The two hardest unresolved questions are now: 1. How is the relevant dimension space discovered? and: 2. What exactly constitutes a valid epistemic determination? I would research those two questions next. And only after that would I return to measure theory and ask: Which parts of this process genuinely require measure-theoretic probability, and which do not? That prevents us from making the mathematics drive the ontology.
b_rows_sample.statement: Names the two hardest unresolved questions to research next: (1) how is the relevant dimension space discovered, and (2) what exactly constitutes a valid epistemic determination; only after resolving those should the research return to measure theory and ask which parts of the process genuinely require measure-theoretic probability and which do not -- explicitly to prevent the mathematics from driving the ontology.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Q1: What exactly is a "state"? ... Q2: Is every fact a dimension? ... Q3: Can dimensions themselves change? ... S_t -> S_{t+1} vs. D_t -> D_{t+1} ... Q4: What determines relevance of a dimension? Relevance(d | Context, Question, Purpose, Rules). But this is a hypothesis, not a definition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Poses four unresolved questions about the state/dimension ontology: Q1 what exactly is a 'state' (physical/software/business-process/institutional/propositional/knowledge-state, and can it contain entities/relationships/events/rules/capabilities/intentions/constraints); Q2 is every fact a dimension, or is the dimension-value pair distinct from the dimension itself, and does every relationship constitute a separate dimension; Q3 can dimensions themselves change (distinguishing state change S_t->S_{t+1} from dimension-model change D_t->D_{t+1}); Q4 what determines the relevance of a dimension, hypothesized as Relevance(d | Context, Question, Purpose, Rules) but not yet a definition. All marked Status: Undefined.

group_evidence.why_grouped: an UNKNOWN-OBJECT-CANDIDATE row (batch B0055, source S2263) named these as alternative candidates for one piece of evidence. why_uncertain: Restates a Ch1-2 observation/dimension-discovery/recalculation pipeline that likely maps onto the pre-existing dimension-discovery-capability object from B0019.
working_label token overlap Jaccard=0.50 (shared tokens: ['dimension', 'discovery'])

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1}=Revise(K_t,E_{new}) ... H_{t+1}\supseteq H_t ... current state may change without destroying the history
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates the revision model K_{t+1}=Revise(K_t,E_new) alongside additive history H_{t+1}⊇H_t, so current state can change without destroying its historical derivation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: RevisionType=\{Evolution,Correction,Retraction,Refutation,Reinterpretation,ModelRevision\}
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a six-value RevisionType taxonomy for 'something previously accepted is later discovered to be wrong': Evolution, Correction, Retraction, Refutation, Reinterpretation, ModelRevision — argued to require distinct treatment since collapsing them into one Boolean 'wrong' loses epistemic information; recommended as part of the domain language.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A_1\rightarrow A_2 if an actual upgrade occurred ... Evolution\neq Correction. The old knowledge remains historically valid
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Evolution: a genuine world state change (A1 at t1 -> A2 at t2) where the first assertion was true when made — Evolution ≠ Correction, old knowledge remains historically valid.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Correction(E_1,E_2) ... Status(E_1)=Corrected ... a new event rather than a destructive modification
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Correction: a source reporting its own earlier record was a typo/error is represented as Correction(E1,E2) with Status(E1)=Corrected, the original event remaining in history as a new event rather than a destructive modification.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Support(A)\downarrow but does not necessarily establish \neg A ... Retraction\neq Refutation ... especially important for statistical reasoning
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Retraction: a source withdrawing support lowers Support(A) but does not establish ¬A — Retraction ≠ Refutation, 'losing support for a hypothesis is not automatically equivalent to proving the hypothesis false' — 'especially important for statistical reasoning.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: A\perp B ... if new evidence is sufficiently authoritative, A may be classified as Refuted ... refutation is a conclusion derived from evidence and domain semantics; it is not merely the existence of a second assertion
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Refutation: when a domain model treats two same-context/time assertions as mutually exclusive (A⊥B) and new evidence is sufficiently authoritative, A may be classified Refuted — a conclusion derived from evidence plus domain semantics, not merely a second assertion existing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: command was actually executed against the development system ... ObservationValid\land AssertionInvalid ... exactly why the layered model from 25I is necessary
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Reinterpretation: an observation can remain valid while the derived assertion is wrong (e.g. a command result correctly observed but wrongly attributed to production instead of development) — ObservationValid ∧ AssertionInvalid — explicitly validating the necessity of S0901's layered Observation/Representation/Assertion model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: HasIP(Server,x) is functional ... Later we correct the domain model ... \Omega_1\rightarrow\Omega_2 ... K^{\Omega_1}\neq K^{\Omega_2} ... ModelRevision ... historical interpretation under \Omega_1 must remain reproducible
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines ModelRevision using the IP-address-functionality example: the underlying observations are unchanged but a domain-model correction (Omega1->Omega2) changes the interpretation (K^Omega1 ≠ K^Omega2); the historical Omega1-based interpretation must remain reproducible.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K^{(1)}=Derive(H,\Omega_1) and K^{(2)}=Derive(H,\Omega_2) ... Interpretation is versioned
a_rows_sample.statement: States KnowledgeOS should answer both 'what did the system conclude under model version 1.0?' and '...under model version 2.0?' via K^(1)=Derive(H,Omega1), K^(2)=Derive(H,Omega2) — 'Interpretation is versioned.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: H'=H\cup\{E_{revision}\} ... K'=Derive(H',\Omega,EC,M) ... Revision=EventAddition+StateReDerivation ... considerably cleaner than destructive updates
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes revision as operating through the event history rather than direct mutation: H'=H∪{E_revision}, K'=Derive(H',Omega,EC,M) — Revision = EventAddition + StateReDerivation, 'considerably cleaner than destructive updates.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: E_1:Nexus=3.70 followed by E_2:Correction(E_1,3.69) ... K_{current}=3.69 ... can still reconstruct K_{before correction}=3.70 ... nothing historically meaningful has been erased
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: after a correction event, the system derives current state 3.69 while still being able to reconstruct the pre-correction state 3.70 — 'nothing historically meaningful has been erased.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Assessment(A): Strong\rightarrow Weak ... Assertion\neq Assessment
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: discovering an unreliable measurement method changes an assertion's support Assessment (Strong->Weak) without refuting the proposition itself — Assertion ≠ Assessment, flagged as important for the upcoming formal evidence-aggregation step.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(H\mid E_1)=0.95 ... P(H\mid E_1,E_2)=0.40 ... has not logically been proven false ... Probability revision\neq Logical refutation ... must not invent priors or probability models implicitly
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked numerical example (P(H|E1)=0.95 dropping to P(H|E1,E2)=0.40) shows substantially reduced support without logical refutation — Probability revision ≠ Logical refutation; permits Bayesian updating P(H|E1,E2) ∝ P(E2|H,E1)P(H|E1) where an explicit probabilistic model exists, but warns the system must not implicitly invent priors or probability models.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ValidFrom\le t<ValidUntil ... KnowledgeOS must support both DeterministicModels and ProbabilisticModels ... should not reduce the entire KnowledgeState to a probability distribution
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms deterministic and probabilistic knowledge coexist (e.g. validity-interval evaluation needs no probability) — KnowledgeOS must support both, not reduce everything to a probability distribution.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence E1->Assertion A1->Knowledge K1->Requirement R1->Zero->Lord->Decision D1 ... Revision propagation=Support recomputation, not cascading deletion
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked dependency-chain example: retracting E1 must propagate through Assertion->Knowledge->Requirement->Zero->Lord->Decision without deleting downstream state; if A1 also has independent support E2, retracting E1 may weaken but not destroy A1 — 'Revision propagation = Support recomputation, not cascading deletion.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: RF(E) ... Recalculate(RF(E)) ... an incremental computation strategy rather than requiring the entire knowledge graph to be rebuilt
