Traced only in STEP-TRACE-B1/B2/B3. No mandate's coverage requirement reaches them, and I flagged this twice without acting on
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the 198 non-step files (42% of the corpus, including the Q-series Q1-Q24) as the programme's most consequential coverage gap: it was traced only in three STEP-TRACE files, no mandate's coverage requirement reaches it, and it is exactly where this same session's S1605 finding (the assertion layer already established in Q7) was located -- the verifier explicitly notes flagging this coverage hole twice previously without acting on it.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Add, Remove, Revise, Merge, Split, Supersede, Validate, Reject, Transform. ... What invariants survive these operations?
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 232 (tail) asks whether knowledge states form an algebraic structure under nine operations (Add, Remove, Revise, Merge, Split, Supersede, Validate, Reject, Transform), posing Add(K,x)?, Merge(K1,K2)?, Revise(K,x,x')?, Transform(K_A,C_A,C_B)?, and the key question of what invariants survive these operations.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathbb K=\{(G,\sigma,\theta,\lambda,\pi)\mid \text{state satisfies the domain invariants}\}. ... (\mathbb K,\mathcal O)
b_rows_sample.statement: The knowledge-state SPACE mathbb K (all admissible states satisfying domain invariants) is distinguished from a particular STATE mathfrak K_t at time t; rather than assuming a classical algebraic structure (ring/field/vector space), the appropriate initial object is a state-transition algebra (mathbb K, mathcal O) where mathcal O is the set of admissible operations.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Transformation\neq Validation. Validation:\mathbb K\times X\rightarrow Assessment while Transformation:\mathbb K\times Parameters\rightarrow\mathbb K.
b_rows_sample.statement: State-changing vs state-classifying operations: Transformation != Validation -- Validation: mathbb K x X -> Assessment (may merely produce an assessment) while Transformation: mathbb K x Parameters -> mathbb K (changes the state); validation may subsequently trigger a transition, corresponding to the DDD chain Command->Decision->Event->State, rated a much better model than treating CRUD as the architecture.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Add_x(\mathfrak K) is a partial operation. ... Remove_x:\mathbb K\rightharpoonup\mathbb K. ... Remove(E) may require Reassess(A).
b_rows_sample.statement: Addition Add_x:mathbb K -> mathbb K is a PARTIAL operation, defined only if Invariant(K')=True; Removal Remove_x:mathbb K -|-> mathbb K is likewise partial since an accepted item may depend on the removed one (A-dependsOn->E), so Remove(E) may require Reassess(A).

b_rows_sample.anchor: x_t\xrightarrow{revisedTo}x_{t+1}. Revision=new state+historical relation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Revision must not be modeled as overwriting (x_t <- x_{t+1}, destroying history) but as x_t -revisedTo-> x_{t+1}, giving Revision = new state + historical relation, naturally supporting lineage.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \sigma(x_1)=Superseded and \sigma(x_2)=Accepted. Currentness\neq Truth.
b_rows_sample.statement: Supersession differs from revision: x1 is retained as historical knowledge marked Superseded (sigma(x1)=Superseded) while x2 is Accepted, again demonstrating Currentness != Truth.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Merge\neq SetUnion. ... Merge(K_1,K_2,C,P) ... compatible, redundant, complementary, contradictory, superseding. ... TextMerge\neq SemanticMerge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Merge is a partial, semantic operation Merge:mathbb K x mathbb K -|-> mathbb K, not naive set union (Merge != SetUnion) since sources may contain contradictory claims; a proper Merge(K1,K2,C,P) classifies relationships as compatible/redundant/complementary/contradictory/superseding -- giving the DDD principle TextMerge != SemanticMerge (a repository-level/Git merge is not necessarily a domain merge).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Split(Merge(K_1,K_2))\neq(K_1,K_2). ... non-invertible knowledge transformation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Split:mathbb K -|-> mathbb K x mathbb K is not a true mathematical inverse of Merge -- Split(Merge(K1,K2)) != (K1,K2) in general because merge may introduce derived information, reconciliation decisions, normalization, or conflict resolution -- an example of non-invertible knowledge transformation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: (\mathcal T,\circ) has the structure of a transformation semigroup, assuming closure. ... (\mathcal T,\circ,I) is at least monoid-like. ... We should not claim it yet as a theorem.
b_rows_sample.statement: The set of admissible transformations mathcal T with composition forms a candidate transformation semigroup (mathcal T, o) assuming closure, with an identity transformation I_K(K)=K making (mathcal T,o,I) at least monoid-like -- explicitly not yet claimed as a proven theorem, but architecturally useful for representing pipelines K3=(T3 o T2 o T1)(K0).

b_rows_sample.anchor: T_2\circ T_1 may be mathematically composable but not governance-valid. MathematicalComposition from GovernedComposition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Governance breaks naive composition: T1 authorized in context C1 composed with T2 (requiring ungranted authority) may be mathematically composable but not governance-valid, requiring MathematicalComposition to be distinguished from GovernedComposition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal T_G\subseteq\mathcal T ... T\in\mathcal T_G only if Authority(T)\land Policy(T)\land RequiredEvidence(T). ... we should not automatically call \mathcal T_G a semigroup.
b_rows_sample.statement: Governed transformations mathcal T_G subseteq mathcal T require Authority(T) and Policy(T) and RequiredEvidence(T); mathcal T_G is NOT necessarily closed under composition (T1,T2 in T_G but T2 o T1 not in T_G if the combined transformation crosses a governance boundary) -- an important mathematical correction against assuming T_G is a semigroup.

b_rows_sample.anchor: G(T,K,C,A,P)\in\{0,1\}. K'=T(K) only if G(T,K,C,A,P)=1. ... Evidence is a condition of admissibility, not merely metadata.
b_rows_sample.statement: Governance is formalized as a boolean constraint system G(T,K,C,A,P) in {0,1}: a state transition K'=T(K) is valid only if G(T,K,C,A,P)=1, and separately E(T) |= ReqEvidence(T,P) must hold -- evidence is a condition of admissibility, not merely metadata. Together these give the core transition rule K_{t+1}=T_t(K_t) subject to G(...)=1 and E_t |= ReqEvidence(T_t,P_t).

b_rows_sample.anchor: M_C(\Delta_t)\Rightarrow Governed(T_t). ... U_t=\varnothing. A governed knowledge system may transform information, but material semantic changes may not occur silently.
b_rows_sample.statement: Material-change condition, rated potentially one of the most important invariants in the entire architecture: M_C(Delta_t)=1 (materiality of the diff between K_t and K_{t+1}) implies Governed(T_t); reformulated elegantly as U_t = empty set where U_t is the set of undeclared material changes -- a governed knowledge system may transform information, but material semantic changes may never occur silently.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t\subseteq K_{t+1} ... Clearly not. ... HistoricalKnowledge(K_t)\subseteq HistoricalKnowledge(K_{t+1}). ... HistoricalMonotonicity.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge is NOT monotonic (K_t subseteq K_{t+1} fails since knowledge can be corrected/withdrawn/superseded/invalidated), but a weaker HistoricalMonotonicity holds: HistoricalKnowledge(K_t) subseteq HistoricalKnowledge(K_{t+1}) -- the system should not erase the fact that a knowledge state existed, even though Current(K_t) need not be monotonic while History(K_<=t) should normally grow.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Do not assume KnowledgeOS is a lattice. It may become a partial order over particular classes of knowledge states, but this requires proof.
b_rows_sample.statement: Whether knowledge states form a lattice under an information ordering K1<=K2 (K2 contains at least as much accepted information) is explicitly left open and cautioned against assuming, since contradictions complicate a least-upper-bound K1 join K2; likewise no universal statistical information ordering should be assumed given multiple incompatible candidates (entropy, KL divergence, Fisher information, posterior concentration).

b_rows_sample.anchor: F_Y=F_X\circ T^{-1}. ... Y must remain linked to X. This is exactly what lineage is supposed to preserve.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distributional transformation is a rigorous statistical-layer example of knowledge transformation: for X~F and measurable T, Y=T(X) induces F_Y = F_X o T^-1; when KnowledgeOS derives an engineering indicator Y from observed metric X, Y must remain linked to X via provenance/uncertainty/assumptions -- exactly what lineage is meant to preserve.

b_rows_sample.anchor: q_1,q_2\xrightarrow{f}q. ... Validity(q)=g(Validity(q_1),Validity(q_2),f).
b_rows_sample.statement: Derived knowledge q=f(q1,q2) gives a knowledge derivation graph q1,q2-f->q; dependency preservation proposes Validity(q) = g(Validity(q1),Validity(q2),f) so that invalidating q1 makes q suspect -- a candidate for deterministic validity propagation, illustrated by Requirement->ArchitectureDecision->ImplementationConstraint where superseding the Requirement triggers Supersession->ImpactAnalysis on the ArchitectureDecision, not necessarily invalidation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Impact(q)=Descendants(q). ... Reassessment(Impact(q)). This may become one of the most important practical capabilities of KnowledgeOS.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge impact propagation: Impact(q) = Descendants(q) in the provenance/semantic graph, so a material change to q triggers Reassessment(Impact(q)) -- rated potentially one of the most important practical capabilities of KnowledgeOS, and making the transformation algebra explicitly dependency-aware: Input+Context+Evidence+Authority+Dependencies -> Output.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Law 1 -- Traceability ... Law 2 -- Governance ... Law 3 -- Evidence ... Law 4 -- Semantic accountability ... Law 5 -- Historical preservation ... Law 6 -- Epistemic separation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Six candidate algebraic laws, rated much closer to architectural invariants than the earlier broad principles: L1 Traceability (exists L(T) for every material transformation), L2 Governance (Material(T)=>Authorized(T)), L3 Evidence (RequiredEvidence(T)=>Evidence(T)), L4 Semantic accountability (MaterialSemanticChange(T)=>Declared(T)), L5 Historical preservation (historical state not silently destroyed), L6 Epistemic separation (Status(q) != Content(q)).

b_rows_sample.anchor: All changes require human approval is a policy. It is not necessarily a universal architectural invariant. ... Every consequential transformation requires an authority mechanism appropriate to its risk and policy.
b_rows_sample.statement: Crucial distinction between invariant and policy: 'all changes require human approval' is a policy, not a universal invariant; the more general, robust invariant is 'every consequential transformation requires an authority mechanism appropriate to its risk and policy' (human approval, delegated authority, deterministic policy, or automated rule).

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 's1605-question-7-assertion-layer-rediscovery' POSSIBLY relates to 'step232-knowledge-state-algebra' (batch B0039). Note: A pre-Step-001 (2026-08-26) non-step corpus file, 'question-7-what-is-knowledge-itself.md', found by this batch's verification chain to already contain the Proposition/Assertion/KnowledgeState three-level type distinction (P=(E,D,V), A=(P,Sigma,E,tau,Pi), K_t as a 6-tuple) that Steps 243-246 independently rediscovered by executed counterexample 219 steps later, after it was lost from the numbered-step corpus; Q7 itself calls collapsing these levels 'the biggest mathematical problem in the document'. Flagged for independent verification of dating/content given the batch's standing caution about provenance-of-establishment claims.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We want to know whether there exists a corresponding state transformation T:K x I -> K such that F(That(H,i)) = T(F(H),i) for every valid H and input i. If this holds, then the history dynamics descend to the state space.
a_rows_sample.statement: Sets up the formal question of state sufficiency: given a history space H, a proposed state abstraction F:H->K, and a history-level transformation That:HxI->H, does a corresponding state-level transformation T:KxI->K exist such that F(That(H,i))=T(F(H),i) for all valid H,i -- i.e. do history dynamics descend to the state space.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H_A ~_F H_B iff F(H_A)=F(H_B). Then state sufficiency requires: H_A ~_F H_B => That(H_A,i) ~_F That(H_B,i). Thus ~_F must be a congruence with respect to valid transformations.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the equivalence relation ~_F induced by the state abstraction (H_A~_F H_B iff F(H_A)=F(H_B)) and states the central congruence requirement: this equivalence must be preserved by every valid transformation for the state representation to be sufficient.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Now suppose the proposed state representation retains only Content(K)={p}. ... Authorized(A)=true but Authorized(B)=false. Then F(That(H_A,validate)) != F(That(H_B,validate)). Yet initially F(H_A)=F(H_B). Content-only K fails the congruence test. This is a genuine falsification.
a_rows_sample.statement: Falsifies a content-only knowledge state via a worked example: two histories with different evidence sources (A authorized, B not) collapse to the same content-only state, but a governance-sensitive validation transformation produces divergent outcomes (Validated vs Unvalidated) depending on the discarded source information -- a genuine congruence failure, showing content-only K is insufficient once authority-sensitive transformations are valid operations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose we enrich the state with lambda(e)=source(e). Now F(H_A) != F(H_B) ... The previous counterexample disappears. But this does not yet prove sufficiency. We have only shown one missing distinction has been restored.
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows adding a source/provenance field lambda(e)=source(e) to the state resolves the specific counterexample found, but explicitly cautions this only restores one missing distinction and does not establish global sufficiency -- more collapsed-but-behaviorally-different histories must still be searched for.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose H_C and H_D have identical Content and Provenance. But H_C was produced under policy pi_1 while H_D was produced under pi_2 ... F(H_C)=F(H_D) under a representation that omits policy history. But T(H_C,i) != T(H_D,i). ... Is Policy part of state, provenance, or external context? ... It is de
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a further counterexample: two histories identical in content and provenance but produced under different policies collapse to the same state under a policy-omitting representation, yet future validation depending on the original governing policy produces different results -- concluding whether policy belongs to state, provenance, or external context cannot be decided by convenience but is determined by transformation sufficiency (independently arriving at a question the parallel verifier track, S1602/S1603, was also attacking).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Two histories have the same proposition but different validity intervals theta_A(p)=[t0,t1), theta_B(p)=[t1,t2). Suppose a transformation asks CurrentVersion(S,t1+epsilon)? Then the two states produce different results. ... Temporal validity is not merely decorative metadata if temporal queries are
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows via a temporal-query counterexample (CurrentVersion(S,t1+epsilon)?) that a state representation omitting temporal qualification fails congruence when temporal queries are valid operations -- confirming temporal validity is functionally load-bearing, not decorative metadata.

a_rows_sample.anchor: e1->p and e2->not p. Compare K_A={p,e1} with K_B={p,e1,e2,not p}. A transformation T_assess may produce Assessment(K_A)=Supported but Assessment(K_B)=Conflicted. ... A state representation containing only the latest proposition K={p} would lose information necessary for future assessment.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a contradictory-evidence counterexample showing evidence multiplicity is semantically relevant: two states differing only in whether conflicting evidence is retained produce different Assessment outcomes (Supported vs Conflicted) under T_assess, so a state keeping only the latest proposition would lose information needed for future assessment.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose an information component x can affect the result of a valid future transformation T(K,i). Then x cannot be discarded from the state abstraction unless it is recoverable from other state information. Formally: x is semantically disposable => x=f(K) for some reconstruction function f, or no va
a_rows_sample.statement: States a general disposability criterion generalizing all the preceding counterexamples: an information component x may be discarded from the state abstraction only if it is reconstructible from the remaining state (x=f(K) for some f) or no valid operation can distinguish states differing only in x -- giving a formal test for classifying any candidate field as state, metadata, provenance, external context, or truly redundant.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K=F(H) is a transformation-sufficient representation if all permitted future semantics can be determined from K, rather than the complete H. But we should not call K a sufficient statistic without qualification. ... K must be sufficient for the permitted KnowledgeOS transformation semantics.
a_rows_sample.statement: Draws an explicit but qualified analogy to the statistical notion of a sufficient statistic: a state K=F(H) is transformation-sufficient if all permitted KnowledgeOS transformation semantics can be determined from K rather than the full history H -- but the file cautions the statistical term applies to a specific model/parameter and should not be borrowed unqualified, since the KnowledgeOS requirement is broader (sufficiency for a whole permitted transformation semantics, not one parameter).

a_rows_sample.anchor: H ~ mu_H. Then K=F(H) induces a push-forward distribution mu_K = F_* mu_H. ... mu_K is a regime-level object, not necessarily part of K.
a_rows_sample.statement: Connects the state abstraction to measure theory without making it foundational: if H is a random history with distribution mu_H, then K=F(H) induces a push-forward distribution mu_K=F_*mu_H (mu_K(A)=mu_H(F^{-1}(A)) for measurable A); explicitly classifies mu_K as a regime-level object, consistent with the parallel Step 246 finding (S1601) that probability belongs to a regime projection, not to K itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: F is a compression map. The question becomes: Is this compression lossless with respect to the semantics we care about? That is exactly the congruence question. ... F o That = T o F. This is the formal expression of state sufficiency.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the commutative-diagram criterion F o That = T o F as the formal expression of state sufficiency (the state abstraction F is a compression map; sufficiency means the compression is lossless with respect to the transformation semantics), calling it one of the strongest formal tests obtained in the corpus so far, and gives the corresponding failure interpretation (a non-commuting diagram means the proposed state representation has lost necessary information).

a_rows_sample.anchor: K=(Content,Qualification,Governance) survives the experiments only if those components contain all information required by valid transformations. ... we should not yet assert K=(G,sigma,theta,lambda,pi) as a final decomposition. Instead: K must be defined by transformation sufficiency. This reverses
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the design question from 'what fields should a Knowledge State have?' to 'what information must a state preserve so that all valid KnowledgeOS transformations remain well-defined?'; explicitly withholds asserting K=(G,sigma,theta,lambda,pi) as final until it survives transformation-sufficiency testing -- a route to the same skepticism about the 5-tuple that the parallel verifier track reached by counterexample.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Minimality = systematic removal + congruence testing. This is far stronger than selecting the smallest-looking tuple. ... Minimality is always relative to the transformation language. ... Minimality(K) = Minimality(K | T). There may be no context-free 'minimal Knowledge State.'
a_rows_sample.statement: Reformulates minimality testing as systematic per-component removal followed by re-checking the congruence criterion (F^{-i} o That = T^{-i} o F^{-i}), rather than choosing the smallest-looking tuple by inspection; states the important architectural corollary that minimality is always relative to the transformation language T (Minimality(K)=Minimality(K|T)) -- there may be no context-free minimal Knowledge State, since a richer future transformation set can make previously-discardable information necessary.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Transformation-Sufficiency Proposition: T:K x I -> K is semantically well-defined with respect to That iff F(H1)=F(H2) => F(That(H1,i))=F(That(H2,i)) for all valid H1,H2,i. Equivalently F o That = T o F. ... not yet a proven KnowledgeOS theorem, because the full transformation set has not been estab
a_rows_sample.statement: States the phase's central named proposition (Transformation-Sufficiency Proposition), giving a single precise, computationally testable mathematical criterion for when a state-level transformation is semantically well-defined relative to a history-level one -- explicitly labeled not yet a proven theorem because the full KnowledgeOS transformation set has not itself been established.

a_rows_sample.anchor: PASS -- Transformation congruence criterion established. FAIL -- Global state sufficiency not yet demonstrated. OPEN -- Minimal sufficient Knowledge State. ... K should not be defined independently of T. Instead, the pair (K,T) must be reconstructed together.
a_rows_sample.statement: Records the Step-248 verdict: PASS on establishing the congruence criterion; FAIL on demonstrating global state sufficiency; OPEN on minimal sufficient K; states the phase's major conceptual shift -- K must not be designed independently of the transformation set T, but the pair (K,T) must be reconstructed jointly -- and sets Step 249 as Transformation Algebra Reconstruction, to derive the corpus-supported transformation classes (T_create, T_observe, T_infer, T_validate, T_revise, T_reject, T_merge, T_supersede, ...) with domain/codomain/preconditions/postconditions/invariants/composability for each.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Can two states with identical current representation produce different valid future behavior? ... If T(K_A)=K'_A and T(K_B)=K'_B with K'_A not equiv K'_B, then history affects future semantics. In that case, the compressed state K is not sufficient. This gives us a rigorous state sufficiency criteri
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the provenance-metadata-vs-constitutive question into a testable future-behavior criterion avoiding philosophical argument: if two states with identical current representation but different history produce different results under the same transformation, then the state representation is insufficient -- directly the criterion S1608 (Step 248) then executes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose they produce identical lineage edges. Yet the transformations had different policies pi_A != pi_B. If policy is semantically relevant, then lambda_A=lambda_B does not imply H_A = H_B. ... Potentially lambda=(source,transformation,actor,time,policy,evidence). But this is again a candidate str
a_rows_sample.statement: Falsifies plain parent-child lineage as a sufficient history compression: two histories can produce identical lineage edges while having been governed by different policies, so if policy is semantically relevant then lineage-equality does not imply history-equivalence -- proposing a richer candidate lambda=(source,transformation,actor,time,policy,evidence), still only a candidate structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: That requires: H_1 ~_H H_2 => T(H_1) ~_H T(H_2). This is a congruence condition. If it holds, the transformation descends from histories to states. ... State abstraction is valid only if it is transformation-compatible.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the congruence condition required for the equivalence-class definition of Knowledge State to be usable: ~_H must be preserved by every valid transformation (H1~_H H2 => T(H1)~_H T(H2)), so that transformations descend consistently from histories to their equivalence classes -- directly foreshadowing S1608's F o That = T o F criterion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What is the smallest mathematical structure that satisfies all non-negotiable requirements? Construct a sequence K0 -> K1 -> K2 -> ... where each added component must have a demonstrated necessity. ... The final result must distinguish MINIMALITY PROVEN from MINIMALITY PLAUSIBLE from MINIMALITY NOT
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes a 'minimal adequate K' procedure: build up a sequence K0->K1->K2->... adding only demonstrably-necessary components (tested against 7 questions per candidate: forcing requirement, external representability, derivability, removal breakage, reconstructability, circularity, unwanted coupling), and introduces a 3-level minimality-confidence taxonomy (PROVEN / PLAUSIBLE / NOT ESTABLISHED) explicitly rejecting fewer-fields as a minimality argument -- complementing S1608's congruence-based removal test with a positive constructive procedure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We cannot yet remove Merge, Supersede, Split, Withdraw because the corpus may require them for capabilities that have not yet been tested. Therefore the minimality status is: NOT YET TESTABLE rather than: minimal set found.
a_rows_sample.statement: Declares minimality of the state-changing operation family NOT YET TESTABLE (not merely unresolved), since Merge/Supersede/Split/Withdraw cannot yet be safely removed given untested capability requirements -- consistent with S1608's mandate that minimality testing requires actual removal-and-congruence checks, not inspection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We must distinguish at least three relations: =_X object equality, equiv_K Knowledge-State equivalence, ~_H history equivalence. They answer different questions ... These must not be collapsed into one relation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes 3 distinct sameness relations for KnowledgeOS -- object equality (are two knowledge objects the same per the object model), Knowledge-State equivalence (are two states indistinguishable for all semantically relevant operations), and history equivalence (are two histories equivalent with respect to resulting semantic behavior) -- explicitly forbidding their collapse into one relation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: x1=(id=42,content=A) and x2=(id=42,content=B). They may represent different versions of the same knowledge entity. Identity persistence != value equality. This is exactly what Revision requires.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proves identity persistence and value equality are distinct via a minimal worked example (same id, different content = two versions of the same entity), noting this is exactly the distinction Revision requires to exist.

b_rows_sample.anchor: x=(i,v,s,p,m) [identity, value, status, provenance, metadata] -- not yet the final Knowledge Object definition. It is a diagnostic model. ... =_I identity equality, =_V content equality, =_S full structural equality, =_E semantic equality [the least trivial to define].
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a diagnostic (not final) 5-field Knowledge Object model x=(identity,value,status,provenance,metadata) and defines 4 candidate object-equality relations over it (identity-only, content-only, full-structural, and semantic equality -- the last flagged as most important and least trivial to define).

b_rows_sample.anchor: =_I cannot by itself be the semantic equality relation [fails Revise, which requires semantic change while identity persists]. ... Content equality cannot replace identity [fails Merge/Supersede, which must distinguish independently-created identical-content objects].
b_rows_sample.statement: Proves both identity-only equality and content-only equality are individually insufficient as the semantic equality relation: identity-only equality cannot represent Revise (which needs semantic change while identity persists); content-only equality cannot represent Merge/Supersede (which must distinguish two independently-created objects with identical content).

b_rows_sample.anchor: K1 equiv_K K2 iff no mandatory KnowledgeOS observation or transformation can distinguish them. Formally: forall O in mathcal-O: O(K1)=O(K2). For transitions we need the stronger congruence condition: K1 equiv_K K2 => T(K1,c) equiv_K T(K2,c) for all admissible common contexts c.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Knowledge-State equivalence observationally (agreement on every semantically relevant observation), then states the stronger transformation-congruence requirement that equivalence must be preserved by every valid transformation -- the critical test for whether the proposed equivalence is too coarse.

b_rows_sample.anchor: H1 ~_H H2 iff all permitted future operation sequences produce equivalent states. Formally, for every admissible sequence sigma=Tn o ... o T1, we require F(sigma(H1)) equiv_K F(sigma(H2)). ... If sim_H is a valid behavioral equivalence relation, then Knowledge State can potentially be understood as
b_rows_sample.statement: Strengthens history equivalence beyond the naive current-state-collapse definition into full behavioral equivalence (agreement of outcomes under every admissible future operation sequence, not just the current state), reaffirming Step 247's (S1609) candidate quotient definition K=[H]_{~_H} as a powerful but still unproven formulation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: F(H1)=F(H2) iff H1 ~_H H2 would mean that the state representation exactly captures the behavioral equivalence classes. That would be a major theoretical result. We have not demonstrated this yet.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the ideal biconditional quotient criterion (F(H1)=F(H2) iff H1 and H2 are behaviorally equivalent) as the major unproven theoretical result the whole state-abstraction programme is aiming at.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Counterexample class A (provenance) ... if a future operation TraceOrigin(x) must return different results, H1 not-similar H2. ... Different provenance does not automatically imply different Knowledge State. Class B (revision history): conditional on ExplainRevision being required. Class C (identity
b_rows_sample.statement: Applies the counterexample-class methodology (from S1621) to 4 specific classes -- provenance, revision history, identity-vs-content, identity-vs-status -- each showing content-only or identity-only state abstractions fail whenever some mandatory operation actually observes the discarded distinction, with each case's status remaining conditional on which operations are mandatory.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Identity -> Object equality -> State equality/equivalence -> Behavioral/history equivalence. But this should not be interpreted as a strict mathematical hierarchy where each relation is automatically derived from the previous one. They are separate semantic constructs connected by explicit rules.
b_rows_sample.statement: Presents a suggestive but explicitly non-derivational ordering of 4 sameness concepts (identity, object equality, state equivalence, behavioral/history equivalence), warning against treating it as a strict hierarchy where each is automatically derivable from the last -- they remain separate constructs connected only by explicit rules.

b_rows_sample.anchor: OperationalIdentity(x) if exists T in T such that changing id(x) can change T(K,c). ... Relevant(p) if there exists a mandatory operation T and states K1,K2 differing only in p such that T(K1,c) not-equiv_K T(K2,c). Then p cannot be discarded from the semantic state representation unless it is suppl
b_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes identity-relevance into a fully general 'operational relevance' test for any candidate property p: p is Relevant if some mandatory operation and a pair of states differing only in p produce non-equivalent outcomes, in which case p cannot be discarded from the semantic state unless supplied externally -- giving a single principled, uniform criterion applicable to identity, provenance, policy, evidence, or any other candidate field.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K* = minimum information sufficient to preserve all mandatory behavioral distinctions. Not: K*=everything ever observed. And not: K*=smallest tuple someone can invent. This is the mathematically meaningful notion of minimality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Transition Types: Additive (delta_+) ASSERT/LINK, op.claim not-in R, guarantee EVal(...).Boundary=EXPLICIT ; Revision (delta_rev) REVISE/REFACTOR, op.target in R, R' retains old claim and adds SUPERSEDES edge from p_new to p_old ; Retraction (delta_-) RETRACT, op.target in R, updates S+ and S- standing without pruning historical nodes.
a_rows_sample.statement: Classifies transitions into three operational classes with distinct preconditions/guarantees: Additive (ASSERT/LINK, appends new claims/edges monotonically, resulting boundary EXPLICIT), Revision (REVISE/REFACTOR, retains the old claim and adds a SUPERSEDES edge from the new to the old rather than overwriting), and Retraction (RETRACT, updates the standing pair without physically deleting the node).

a_rows_sample.statement: Asserts a reversibility postulate: for every transition delta there exists an inverse delta^-1 that recovers the prior state from the post-state and metadata trace, but implemented as an appended counter-record (a new transition) rather than as log erasure -- reversibility is achieved by forward-appending an inverse operation, never by deleting history.

b_rows_sample.statement: Extends successor-state semantics to concurrent action sets (successor-state axiom for a concurrent-action fluent), and identifies the 'precondition interaction problem': individually-possible concurrent actions (startMoveLeft, startMoveRight) can be jointly impossible even though each satisfies its own precondition axiom, requiring additional interaction constraints beyond the individual precondition axioms.

b_rows_sample.statement: Restates Reiter's formal ontology and axioms (already captured in S2536) under an explicit [EXT]/'extracted not endorsed' framing, emphasizing two carried-forward limitations for any KnowledgeOS transfer: the induction axiom is second-order (not fully first-order decidable), and the successor-state axiom rests on an unproven causal-completeness ASSUMPTION about the axiomatiser's own knowledge, not a theorem.

a_rows_sample.statement: DERIVATION VERDICT PARTIALLY_VALID. I(A)<I(E) presupposes a total order on information content; I_required-I_preserved presupposes an interval scale; neither is established (Section 208.10 explicitly declines to establish one, then uses the operations anyway) -- every downstream claim quantifying loss is conditional on repairing this. Second defect: P(G)=P(A)∪P(E), boxed as 'provenance must be closed under semantic transformation,' is either vacuous (if closure holds, P(A)∪P(E)=P(A)) or self-refuting (if it does not, provenance is not closed); it also excludes any provenance contributed by the governance act itself, directly conflicting with Step 209 Section 209.4's Final(D) ⇒ DecisionBasis(D) ∧ Authority(D) (see Contradiction #2).

a_rows_sample.statement: Statistically, Section 208.6's sufficient-statistic analogy is immediately and correctly fenced ('this is an analogy, not a claim that DDD contracts are literally sufficient statistics') but left un-cashed (no Fisher-Neyman factorization or formal criterion transposed), and Section 208.23's handling of conflicting estimates is sound but uncited against prior statistical steps (025N, 082). a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #2 — Provenance composition (208) excludes the authority Step 209 requires
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 208 Section 208.25 asserts as an equality P(G)=P(A)∪P(E), boxed as 'provenance must be closed under semantic transformation.' b_rows_sample.anchor: DDD CATEGORY ERROR IN THE 'Owner' COLUMN
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 206 Section 206.15 derives the candidate bounded-context set as Observation, Evidence, Assessment, Governance, Decision, Execution. Step 210's Owner column instead contains values like 'Domain' (a layer), 'Persistence/Domain' (two layers), 'Knowledge infrastructure' (a layer), 'Assessment/Contracts' (half artifact-kind), 'Aggregate' (a tactical pattern, not a party), and 'Contracts' (an artifact kind). Only 4 of 15 invariants (I5, I7, I8, I12) have a single, named bounded-context owner; seven (I1, I2, I3, I11, I13, I14, I15) have an owner entirely outside the derived context set, making them ownerless invariants under Step 212's own Section 212.15 criterion; five (I2, I4, I6, I9, I10) have slash-shared owners, Step 212's own Section 212.16 shared-ownership problem.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 210's matrix instantiates, in 12 of its 15 rows, the two failure modes Step 212 names two files later — and neither file notices
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 212 Section 212.15 warns explicitly against 'Ownerless Invariants' (I exists but Owner(I) = empty set), yet Step 212 Section 212.4 reprints the same 15 invariants from Step 210 with the Owner column deleted entirely, and performs no such search -- discarding the exact data (Step 210's Owner column, with 7/15 ownerless and 5/15 shared) that would have triggered Step 212's own diagnosis.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Further arithmetic checks: 0.87>=0.80 correct; 0.91+/-0.08 within range at 1 sigma but 2-sigma bound exceeds 1; ratio checks disclaimed
b_rows_sample.statement: Additional independently-verified arithmetic in the band: Step 209 Section 209.15's 0.87 >= 0.80 evaluates to True (correct). Step 208 Section 208.14 / Step 210 Section 210.12's 0.91 +/- 0.08 gives [0.83, 0.99], within [0,1] at 1-sigma, but at 2-sigma the upper bound is 1.07 > 1 -- out of range for a quantity called 'confidence', though the corpus never commits this specific error since the interval's coverage level is left unlabelled. Step 215 Section 215.24's ratios (182/43=4.233, 43/17=2.529, 17/8=2.125, 8/4=2.0, total 45.5x) make no arithmetic claim and are correctly disclaimed as unknown. Step 209 Section 209.42 vs Step 210 Section 210.25: |I_KOS|=8 vs |{I1..I15}|=15, difference 7, mapping absent (unreconciled).

b_rows_sample.anchor: PREVIOUS DEPENDENCY: 1 (Step 208 only); LATER RESPONSE: Step 210 replaces I_KOS with I1-I15 without amendment
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 209 cites exactly one prior step (Step 208) and zero prior invariant families. Later response in scope: Step 210 Section 210.25 replaces the 8-member I_KOS with a 15-row I1-I15 without amendment; Step 210 Section 210.9 restates Step 209's Section 209.25 semantic-strength principle as Strength(T(x))>Strength(x) requires Justified(T); Step 212 Section 212.4 reprints I1-I15.

b_rows_sample.anchor: FORMAL OBJECTS: Architectural Principle != Architectural Property; V_i=(I_i,O_i,E_i,M_i,T_i,F_i); Referential Integrity < Semantic Historical Integrity
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 210 ('Invariant Verification Matrix') defines a 6-tuple V_i=(I_i,O_i,E_i,M_i,T_i,F_i) per invariant; boxes 'Architectural Principle != Architectural Property' and 'No claim of architectural compliance without identifiable evidence'; defines Reachable(D,E)!=empty; boxes 'Referential Integrity < Semantic Historical Integrity' and 'Epistemic state cannot be silently strengthened'; states Strength(T(x))>Strength(x) requires Justified(T); boxes 'Quantitative value without relevant uncertainty may constitute semantic loss'; defines a statistical-result 8-tuple A=(theta-hat,Estimator,Sample,Population,Model,Assumptions,Uncertainty,Validity); boxes 'Documentation < ExecutableEvidence < FormalProof'; a conceptual Assurance(I)=f(Evidence,Coverage,Independence,Repeatability,Criticality); an E_1..E_5 evidence hierarchy (documentation..formal verification); the target for-all-s-in-S_reachable: I(s)=True; and boxes 'AI may assist assurance; AI should not be the sole source of assurance', plus the 15-row invariant-verification matrix itself (60/60 cells filled).

b_rows_sample.anchor: LATER RESPONSE IN SCOPE: Step 211 reverses Test/Evidence order; Step 212 drops the Owner column and recalibrates E_n
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 210 cites only Step 209 by number ('up to Step 209, we have asked...'). Later response: Step 211 Section 211.2 restates the assurance chain with Test before Evidence, contradicting Step 210's own Section 210.40; Step 212 Section 212.4 reprints I1-I15 minus the Owner column; Step 212 Section 212.6 re-mints an E_0..E_5 scale with different rung definitions than Step 210 Section 210.30's E_1..E_5.

b_rows_sample.anchor: EVOLUTION/DEFINITION VERDICT: CLEAR on the principle/property distinction, CONTRADICTORY on E_1..E_5 (twice)
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 210 answers 'where' (role names) and 'how proven' (test names) but not 'is it true' for any invariant. CLEAR: the principle/property distinction (its best contribution), Referential Integrity < Semantic Historical Integrity, the three assurance levels. INCOMPLETE: V_i is 6-ary, only 3 components ever instantiated. AMBIGUOUS: 'Owner' is used as bounded context, layer, pattern, and team interchangeably. CONTRADICTORY: E_1..E_5 vs Step 212's E_0..E_5 (Contradiction #3), and E_1 bound to two incompatible types within Step 210 itself (Contradiction #4: Section 210.20's evidence-item E_1 vs Section 210.30's documentation-rung E_1).

b_rows_sample.anchor: FIRST INVALID INFERENCE: Section 210.30 vs 210.20 (E_n ambiguity); honest gaps in 210.26/210.28/210.29
b_rows_sample.statement: Section 210.20 uses E_1⇒P and E_2⇒¬P as evidence items; Section 210.30, ten sections later, binds E_1=documentation...E_5=formal verification as evidence-strength levels -- the same subscripted symbol carries two incompatible types with no disambiguation, and every downstream use of E_n in Steps 212-214 inherits the ambiguity. Section 210.29 honestly declines to scalarize Assurance and names fake precision (Assurance=97.3%) as a hazard, yet Section 210.28 immediately prior writes Critical(I)⇒HigherAssurance(I), a comparison requiring the very ordering Section 210.29 declines. Section 210.26 correctly concedes a test provides evidence, not proof (Test(I_8)=PASS does not prove I_8=True in all states), then Section 210.32's target for-all s in S_reachable: I(s)=True leaves S_reachable undetermined (Section 210.33 concedes this openly) -- an honest, correctly-labelled gap, not an invalidity.

b_rows_sample.anchor: COMPUTABILITY: highest rung reached is INPUTS_KNOWN, for I_i/O_i as strings only; 15 tests specified, 0 run
b_rows_sample.statement: V_i is DEFINED with 3/6 components at INPUTS_KNOWN (role-name granularity); the I1-I15 matrix is DEFINED->INPUTS_KNOWN (names) but not CONSTRUCTIBLE (no mechanism/code/test); Assurance(I) is DEFINED but explicitly barred from numeric evaluation; S_reachable is DEFINED but conceded as the open challenge, not CONSTRUCTIBLE. The highest rung reached anywhere in Step 210 is INPUTS_KNOWN, and only for I_i and O_i as strings. TEST VERDICT NOT_EXECUTED: 15 tests specified by name, 0 written, 0 run; Section 210.16's negative test ('can an AI-generated Assessment directly invoke an execution command? Expected: False') is designed in prose and never run against anything.

b_rows_sample.anchor: STATISTICAL VERDICT: STRONG (the 8-tuple A=(theta-hat,...,Validity) is the best statistical section in the band); two correct refusals and two measurement violations
b_rows_sample.statement: Section 210.13's 8-tuple statistical result A=(theta-hat,Estimator,Sample,Population,Model,Assumptions,Uncertainty,Validity) is correct and genuinely good statistical practice, rarely done in architecture documents, but never carried into the matrix (which collapses all eight back into one row) and never connected to the corpus's prior statistical steps (025N, 074, 082, uncited). Correct refusals: Section 210.29 declines to scalarize Assurance (names fake precision explicitly); Section 210.27's Documentation<ExecutableEvidence<FormalProof is a properly-used ordinal. Violations: Section 210.28's Critical(I)⇒HigherAssurance(I) compares assurance levels the same file declines to scale; the E_1<...<E_5 ladder (Section 210.30) is re-issued by Step 212 Section 212.6 with different rung contents and an added E_0 -- the same ordinal scale has two incompatible calibrations in the band, making any statement 'we have E_2 evidence' uninterpretable without knowing which file it was written under -- a scale-integrity failure that silently corrupts later aggregation. The 15-row matrix itself carries no scale at all (purely nominal, no arithmetic attempted -- correct).

b_rows_sample.anchor: DDD VERDICT: MIXED — strong distinctions (Architectural Principle != Property; Referential Integrity < Semantic Historical Integrity; Memory/Identity/History split), weak ownership
b_rows_sample.statement: Architectural Principle != Architectural Property is exactly the right DDD-governance move; Referential Integrity < Semantic Historical Integrity (Section 210.5, a foreign key proves existence not that this version was the artifact used) is a real and useful insight; Section 210.39's Memory/Identity/History separation, concluding the current domain object need not carry all history internally, is correct DDD (event sourcing / separate read model), well argued. Against this, the Owner column's category error means only 4/15 invariants have a single bounded-context owner, 7/15 are owned by a layer or pattern (which cannot be accountable), 5/15 are slash-shared, and I13/I14 are owned by 'Aggregate' -- a tactical pattern name is never the answer to 'who is accountable' in DDD.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ASSUMPTIONS / HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS / UNDEFINED SYMBOLS — Step 210
b_rows_sample.statement: Stated: each invariant has exactly one owner; a test name determines a test; enforcement can be located by inspection. Hidden: that the 15 invariants are the right 15 (no derivation from I_KOS's 8, no completeness claim); that S_reachable is finite or tractable (required by the for-all quantifier, false for unbounded state); that Owner and Enforcement are separable -- the matrix drops Enforcement and keeps Owner, implicitly assuming Owner=Enforcement, which Step 211 Section 211.29 later denies ('Invariant->Owner present but Enforcement missing = a design gap'), meaning by Step 211's own criterion all 15 rows of Step 210's matrix are design gaps. Undefined symbols: Justified(T), Strength(x), Critical(I), HigherAssurance(I), Coverage/Independence/Repeatability, S_reachable, Estimator/Sample/Population/Validity, DA's codomain Result.

b_rows_sample.anchor: WHAT SURVIVES / WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE — Step 210, including the word 'Matrix' itself
b_rows_sample.statement: Survives: Architectural Principle != Architectural Property; Referential Integrity < Semantic Historical Integrity; Documentation<ExecutableEvidence<FormalProof; the 8-component statistical result tuple; the refusal of test-as-proof; the refusal to scalarize assurance; the Memory/Identity/History split; the 15 invariant names as a working checklist. Does not survive: the Owner column (11/15 rows unusable); the Verification column as evidence of anything (0/15 executed); V_i as a realized 6-tuple (3/6 realized); E_1..E_5 as a stable scale; and the word 'Matrix' in the title -- a 4-column table realizing 3 of 6 declared dimensions, with no status and no results, is a checklist.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The most damaging collision is E-binding #2 vs #5, which occurs INSIDE ONE FILE (Step 210)
b_rows_sample.statement: Of the twelve distinct bindings of the glyph E catalogued across the band, the most damaging collision is internal to a single file: Step 210 Section 210.20 writes E_1⇒P (an evidence item entailing a proposition), and Step 210 Section 210.30, ten sections later, writes E_1=documentation (the weakest rung of an assurance ladder) -- same symbol, same file, incompatible types, no disambiguation, no notice.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The symbol I is silently rebound between Step 208 (information measure) and Step 209 onward (invariant) with no announcement
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 208 uses I exclusively for an information measure (I(E), I(A), I_required, I_preserved); Step 209 onward uses I exclusively for invariants (I_L, I_C, I_S, I_i, I_identity, I1-I15, I(s)). The rebinding is never announced -- a reader comparing I(C(A)) (Section 208.4, information) to I(s)=True (Section 210.32, an invariant predicate) is reading two different symbols under one glyph.
